This is not a list of diseases to memorize. It is one thinking process you run on every respiratory disorder. Learn the six questions and you can reason through a disease you have never seen. Step 1 Pathophysiology What is going wrong in the lungs? ➜ Step 2 Assessment What clues is the patient giving me? ➜ Step 3 Diagnostics What test confirms my suspicion? ➜ Step 4 Priority Airway? Breathing? Circulation? ➜ Step 5 Interventions What fixes the immediate threat? ➜ Step 6 Teaching What prevents this from recurring? Sort every respiratory patient into one of three buckets first: airflow problem (

Smoking — the single biggest one, responsible for the large majority of cases. Carcinogens in tobacco smoke cause repeated DNA damage in the bronchial lining, and the damaged cells eventually stop repairing correctly. Risk is measured in pack-years (packs per day × years smoked) and starts falling — but never back to zero — after quitting. Secondhand smoke exposure — a nonsmoker living or working with a smoker inhales the same carcinogens. This is why "never smoker" does not mean "no risk." Environmental exposures — radon (the #1 cause in nonsmokers — odorless gas that seeps into basemen

entries.h: Clinical Judgment Question — Why is lung cancer often diagnosed late?
entries.t: Because the lung tissue itself has no pain receptors and the early symptoms look exactly like ordinary smoker's cough or bronchitis. A tumor can grow for a long time in a large, air-filled organ before it blocks enough airway or presses on enough structure to be noticed — and by then it has often spread. Patients (and clinicians) tend to blame the chronic cough, fatigue and weight loss on smoking or aging, so the workup gets delayed. Screening that helps: annual low-dose CT for adults roughly 50–80 years old with a 20+ pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the last 15 year

Chronic cough — a cough that is new, or that has changed in a long-time smoker. The tumor irritates the airway lining. "Changed" is the word that matters on an exam. Hemoptysis — blood in the sputum, from the tumor eroding into airway blood vessels. Weight loss — unintentional loss with anorexia; tumors are metabolically expensive and release cytokines that drive cachexia. A classic late red flag. Fatigue — from anemia, the metabolic demand of the tumor, and poor gas exchange. Recurrent respiratory infections — the same pneumonia in the same lobe over and over. A mass partially blocks a bronch

entries.h: Which finding concerns you most and why?
entries.t: Hemoptysis — and if the patient is actively bleeding a large volume, it is an airway emergency, not just a worrying symptom. Blood in the airway can obstruct ventilation before it ever causes a hemodynamic problem, so the person drowns before they bleed out. It also signals that the tumor has invaded vasculature. Position the patient with the bleeding side down , give oxygen, suction, and get help. On a stable patient, the finding that most changes your suspicion is new hemoptysis plus unintentional weight loss — that combination is cancer until proven otherwise. Also know the "late/spread" cl

Diagnostic Test Why Is It Ordered? Chest X-ray First, cheapest look. Shows a mass, nodule, pleural effusion, or an area of collapsed lung (atelectasis) behind an obstructing tumor. It detects — it never diagnoses. A lesion has to be about 1 cm before it shows up at all. CT Scan Detail and staging. Gives exact size, location, and whether lymph nodes, the mediastinum, chest wall, liver or adrenals are involved — and it maps the route for a biopsy. Often done with IV contrast, so check kidney function and iodine/contrast allergy first. Bronchoscopy Direct look inside the airways with a flexible s

Verify consent — the provider obtains informed consent; the nurse confirms it is signed, dated, and that the patient can explain the procedure in their own words. Consent must be signed before sedation is given. NPO status — usually NPO 4–8 hours beforehand (commonly "nothing after midnight"). Also hold/clarify anticoagulants, check coagulation labs and platelets, remove dentures, and establish IV access. Patient education — explain that they will get moderate sedation and a numbing spray, that a sore throat and hoarseness afterward are normal, that blood-streaked sputum after a biopsy i

To prevent aspiration. The patient receives sedation and a topical anesthetic sprayed on the throat, both of which knock out the gag and cough reflexes that normally keep stomach contents out of the lungs. Food or fluid in the stomach can be regurgitated and inhaled — and aspiration into a lung that is already compromised is exactly what you cannot afford. An empty stomach also gives a clearer view and less vomiting risk.

Respiratory status — rate, effort, breath sounds, and stridor . Laryngeal edema or laryngospasm from the scope can close the airway. Stridor, drooling, or a rising respiratory rate = call for help immediately . Gag reflex — check with a tongue blade against the back of the throat before anything goes in the mouth — including ice chips. Usually returns in 1–2 hours. Bleeding — a small amount of blood-streaked sputum after biopsy is expected; frank red blood, or more than about 30 mL, is not — report it. Oxygenation — continuous pulse oximetry, supplemental O₂ as ordered, and semi-Fowler's

entries.h: Why must the gag reflex return before eating?
entries.t: Because the gag reflex is the body's mechanical guard against aspiration, and the topical anesthetic deliberately turns it off. Without it, food or fluid slides past the larynx and into the trachea without the patient ever coughing or feeling it — a "silent" aspiration. Confirm the gag is intact first, then start with sips of water, then advance.

Bleeding — the pleura and lung are highly vascular. Watch for rising heart rate, falling blood pressure, and chest tube drainage >100 mL/hr or bright red output. Pneumonia — post-op pain makes patients breathe shallowly and avoid coughing, so secretions pool. Prevent it: pain control, incentive spirometry, splinted coughing, early ambulation. Pneumothorax — the pleural space was entered, so air can remain or leak in and collapse the lung. This is why a chest tube usually stays in until the lung re-expands on X-ray.

entries.h: What assessment findings might indicate a pneumothorax?
entries.t: Sudden sharp chest pain and dyspnea with absent or diminished breath sounds on the affected side. Add: hyperresonance on percussion, unequal chest rise, tachypnea, tachycardia, falling SpO₂, and restlessness/anxiety. If it becomes a tension pneumothorax: tracheal deviation AWAY from the affected side, distended neck veins, hypotension, and severe distress — that is a medical emergency requiring immediate needle decompression, not a call-back-later finding. Chest tube quick rules: gentle bubbling in the water seal on exhalation = expected air leak; continuous bubbling = leak in the system, chec

Surgery — wedge resection, lobectomy (one lobe) or pneumonectomy (whole lung). The only potentially curative option, and only for non-small cell cancer caught early enough that the patient's lung function can survive losing tissue. Radiation — shrinks the tumor before surgery, cleans up after it, or relieves obstruction and bone pain. Teach skin care over the treatment field, expect fatigue, and watch for radiation pneumonitis (dry cough, dyspnea, fever weeks later). Chemotherapy — the mainstay for small cell cancer, which is nearly always spread by diagnosis. Nursing focus is myelosuppression

entries.h: Nursing Priority — what concerns arise after a lung resection?
entries.t: Priority is gas exchange and the chest drainage system, because the remaining lung is now doing all the work. Specifically: • Respiratory: SpO₂, breath sounds bilaterally, respiratory rate and effort; semi-Fowler's; incentive spirometry and splinted coughing every hour while awake. • Chest tube (after lobectomy): assess drainage volume and color, water seal, air leak, and insertion site for subcutaneous emphysema (crackling under the skin). • Hemorrhage: drainage >100 mL/hr, tachycardia, hypotension. • Pain: untreated thoracotomy pain leads directly to splinting → atel

Complete the flow: Start DVT forms usually in a deep leg or pelvic vein ➜ Blank 1 a piece breaks off and embolizes — it travels up the vena cava, through the right atrium and right ventricle, and into the pulmonary artery ➜ Blank 2 it lodges and obstructs pulmonary blood flow — that lung segment is still ventilated but no longer perfused ( dead space / V̇/Q̇ mismatch ) ➜ Result Impaired oxygenation hypoxemia, and strain on the right ventricle PE is a perfusion problem wearing a breathing problem's clothes. The alveoli are open and full of air — there is simply no blood arriving to pick the oxy

entries.h: Risk Factors — check the ones that increase clot formation
entries.t: Every one of these maps onto Virchow's triad : stasis of blood, hypercoagulability , and endothelial (vessel wall) injury . If a risk factor hits one of those three, it counts. Surgery — ✅ Yes — hits all three: immobility on the table and after (stasis), tissue trauma (vessel injury), and a post-op inflammatory clotting surge. Orthopedic hip and knee surgery is the highest-risk of all. Smoking — ✅ Yes — damages the endothelial lining and increases platelet stickiness and fibrinogen. Combined with oral contraceptives the risk multiplies rather than adds. Obesity — ✅ Yes — venous stasis in the l

Sudden dyspnea — the hallmark. Abrupt is the key word — the patient can often name the minute it started. Chest pain — sharp and pleuritic — it gets worse with a deep breath, because the infarcted lung segment irritates the pleura. That is different from the crushing, radiating pressure of an MI. Tachycardia — the heart speeds up to compensate for the blocked pulmonary circulation and the falling cardiac output. Often the earliest objective sign. Anxiety — a sense of impending doom. Do not dismiss it as psychological — it is an early sign of cerebral hypoxia. Hemoptysis — blood-streaked sputum

entries.h: Why does a PE cause sudden shortness of breath?
entries.t: Because the blockage is mechanical and instantaneous — blood flow to that part of the lung stops the second the clot wedges in. That region keeps receiving air but gets no blood, so it becomes wasted ventilation (dead space); meanwhile the blood that is still flowing gets crowded into the remaining lung, so it cannot fully oxygenate. The lung also releases mediators that cause reflex bronchoconstriction and reduce surfactant, and the sudden rise in pulmonary vascular resistance strains the right ventricle. Result: severe hypoxemia and air hunger in a patient who was fine ten minutes ago.
Patient has: recent hip replacement · obesity · smoking history · sudden chest pain · hemoptysis

Pulmonary embolism. Three strong risk factors (major orthopedic surgery with immobility, obesity, smoking) plus the classic sudden pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis is the textbook picture. Hip and knee replacement is the single highest-risk surgery for DVT/PE , and the clot usually announces itself in the first days to weeks after the operation. Treat this as PE until imaging says otherwise — do not wait for confirmation to act.

entries.h: What data should be collected immediately?
entries.t: Oxygen saturation — ✅ Yes, first. It is instant, noninvasive, and directly measures the threatened function. Hypoxia drives the entire response. Respiratory rate — ✅ Yes. Tachypnea is one of the most sensitive early signs and needs no equipment at all. Heart rhythm — ✅ Yes. Tachycardia is expected; new right-heart strain patterns or a new arrhythmia signal a large, hemodynamically significant PE. Blood pressure — ✅ Yes. Hypotension is the line between a PE and a massive PE — it is what makes the patient a candidate for thrombolytics. Lung sounds — ✅ Yes , but understand what they will tell you

Because all five together tell you how much of the pulmonary circulation is blocked and whether the patient is still compensating. SpO₂ and respiratory rate size up the gas-exchange failure; heart rate, rhythm and blood pressure size up whether the right ventricle is losing the fight. Every one of them can be obtained in under two minutes at the bedside without waiting on a lab or radiology — and that speed is the whole point, because PE kills within the first hour. While you assess — do these: stay with the patient, raise the head of bed to high-Fowler's, apply oxygen, call the provider/rapid

Test Purpose CT Angiography The definitive test — the gold standard for diagnosing PE. IV contrast lights up the pulmonary arteries and the clot shows up as a filling defect. Nursing: assess kidney function (creatinine/GFR) and iodine-contrast allergy before, hold metformin, and push fluids afterward to flush the contrast. If contrast is contraindicated (renal failure, severe allergy, pregnancy), a V̇/Q̇ scan is used instead. D-Dimer A screening/rule-out blood test that measures a fragment released when a clot breaks down. Normal is roughly <0.50 mcg/mL FEU (assay-dependent). It is very sensit

entries.h: NCLEX Connection — Why should metformin be held before CT angiography?
entries.t: Because IV contrast can injure the kidneys, and if the kidneys stop clearing metformin it accumulates and causes lactic acidosis — which can be fatal. Metformin does not harm the kidney itself; the contrast does. The danger is the combination. Standard practice is to hold metformin at the time of the study and for 48 hours after , then restart only once kidney function has been rechecked and is stable. Also hydrate the patient before and after to protect the kidneys. Watch for lactic acidosis: hyperventilation/Kussmaul breathing, muscle pain, unusual fatigue, abdominal pain, hypotension.

Medication Purpose Heparin (unfractionated, IV) Stops the clot from getting bigger and stops new clots forming — it does not dissolve the clot that is already there. Used IV as a continuous drip for acute PE because it works immediately and can be turned off fast. Monitor aPTT (goal about 1.5–2.5× control, roughly 46–70 seconds) and daily platelets for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Antidote: protamine sulfate . Enoxaparin (Lovenox, LMWH) Same job as heparin — prevents clot extension — but given subcutaneously with a predictable response, so no routine aPTT monitorin

entries.h: Nursing Priority — the MOST important assessment after anticoagulants are started
entries.t: Assess for bleeding — and neurologic status is the piece that must not be missed, because intracranial hemorrhage is the complication that kills. Anticoagulants do not distinguish between the clot you want gone and the clot holding a small vessel closed. • Neuro: new headache, confusion, change in level of consciousness, unequal pupils, one-sided weakness → suspect bleeding in the brain and act immediately. • Overt bleeding: gums, nose, IV sites, hematuria, bloody or tarry stools, hematemesis, unexplained bruising. • Occult bleeding: falling H&H, new abdominal or flank/back

entries.h: 2e · Patient Teaching Framework — why do we teach… ✅
entries.t: Smoking cessation? — Because nicotine and tobacco smoke injure the vessel lining and make blood stickier — damaged endothelium plus increased platelet aggregation and fibrinogen is two-thirds of Virchow's triad in one habit. Risk is multiplied, not just added, when combined with estrogen contraceptives. Compression stockings? — Because graduated external pressure squeezes the superficial veins and pushes blood back toward the heart instead of letting it pool in the calf — it attacks stasis directly. Apply them in the morning before getting out of bed while the legs are least swollen, make sure

COPD causes… leading to… leading to… COPD causes Chronic, not-fully-reversible airflow obstruction — inflamed, narrowed, mucus-filled airways plus loss of the elastic recoil that normally squeezes air out ➜ Leading to Air trapping and hyperinflation — the patient can get air in but cannot get it all out, so stale air stacks up in the lungs ➜ Leading to Impaired gas exchange — chronic hypoxemia and CO₂ retention, increased work of breathing, and eventually cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure)

entries.h: Understand air trapping — it explains almost every COPD finding ⭐
entries.t: Exhalation is normally passive , powered by the elastic recoil of the lung. In COPD that recoil is destroyed and the small airways lose their structural support, so they collapse partway through exhalation and shut the air in behind them. Residual volume rises → the chest sits permanently over-inflated → barrel chest , and each new breath starts from an already-full lung, so tidal volume shrinks. The diaphragm flattens → a flat diaphragm is a mechanically weak diaphragm, so accessory muscles take over and the work of breathing skyrockets — this is why COPD patients lose weight.

entries.h: What is happening in the lungs?
entries.t: The airways themselves are chronically inflamed and drowning in mucus. Long-term irritation makes the mucus-producing glands enlarge and multiply while the cilia that would normally sweep that mucus out are destroyed — so thick secretions sit in the bronchi, narrow them, and block airflow. Clinically it is defined as a productive cough for at least 3 months a year, 2 years in a row . The mucus plugs also make the lungs a perfect culture medium, which is why these patients get infection after infection. Why "blue bloater": mucus-blocked airways mean poor gas exchange → hypoxemia and cyanos

entries.h: What is happening to the alveoli?
entries.t: The alveolar walls are being destroyed, so many small sacs merge into a few large floppy ones. That does two things at once: it wipes out the surface area available for gas exchange, and it destroys the elastic recoil and the tethering that holds small airways open — so the airways collapse on exhalation and trap air. The pulmonary capillary bed is destroyed along with the walls. Smoking is the usual cause; in a young non-smoker with emphysema, think alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency . Why "pink puffer": these patients keep their oxygen levels near-normal for a long time by working extremely hard

entries.h: 3c · Assessment Framework — why each finding happens 🔍
entries.t: Manifestation Why Does It Occur? Barrel Chest Chronic air trapping keeps the lungs hyperinflated, so the rib cage remodels around the extra volume. The anteroposterior diameter increases until it roughly equals the transverse diameter ( 1:1 , normally about 1:2 ). It is a structural, permanent change — a visual record of years of not being able to exhale. Tripod Position Sitting up and leaning forward with the arms braced on the knees or a table anchors the shoulder girdle so the accessory muscles can pull the rib cage open. Normally the pectoral and neck muscles move the arms; when the arms a

entries.h: Why does pursed-lip breathing help COPD patients? ⭐
entries.t: Because it keeps the floppy small airways from collapsing during exhalation, which is exactly the defect in COPD. Breathing out against partially closed lips raises pressure inside the airway above the pressure of the surrounding lung tissue, so the airway stays open long enough to empty. Less trapped air means the next breath starts from a lower, more efficient lung volume. How to teach it: inhale slowly through the nose for about 2 counts, then exhale gently through pursed lips (like blowing out a candle or whistling) for about 4 counts — exhalation roughly twice as long as inhalation . Do n

Test Purpose Chest X-ray Shows the structural consequences of air trapping — hyperinflated lung fields, a flattened diaphragm , increased AP diameter, and a narrow "hanging" heart. It does not diagnose COPD; during an exacerbation its real job is to rule out pneumonia, pneumothorax, and heart failure . PFTs (pulmonary function tests) The test that actually confirms COPD and grades how severe it is. A post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC ratio less than 0.70 establishes fixed airflow obstruction, and the FEV₁ % predicted stages the disease. Key distinction: in COPD the obstruction does not reverse with

Potential complication Why does it happen? Pneumonia Thick retained mucus plus destroyed cilia equals a warm, undrained culture medium. Bacteria that would normally be swept out sit and multiply. Pneumonia is the most common trigger of an acute exacerbation and the most common cause of death in COPD. Prevention: annual influenza vaccine, pneumococcal vaccine, hand hygiene, avoid sick contacts, hydration to thin secretions, and report a change in sputum color or amount early. Atelectasis A mucus plug blocks a bronchiole and the alveoli beyond it collapse because no air can get in to keep them o
Patient arrives with: dyspnea · increased sputum · low SpO₂

entries.h: What should the nurse do first?
entries.t: Sit the patient upright — high-Fowler's or leaning forward on the overbed table — and apply controlled low-flow oxygen titrated to an SpO₂ of 88–92%, then give the prescribed short-acting bronchodilator. Positioning costs nothing, takes two seconds, and immediately improves ventilation; oxygen treats the hypoxemia that is the actual threat to life. Both address B in ABC before anything else. Then, in order: nebulized albuterol (+ ipratropium) → systemic corticosteroid → antibiotics if the sputum has changed color/increased (infection is the usual trigger) → ABG and chest X

Because sitting upright lets gravity pull the abdominal organs downward and away from the diaphragm, so the lungs have room to expand. Lying flat pushes the abdominal contents up against an already flattened, weakened diaphragm and shrinks the space available for air — the exact opposite of what a hyperinflated chest needs. Upright and leaning forward also anchors the shoulder girdle so the accessory muscles can help, and it improves the mechanics of coughing so secretions actually clear. Position first — it is the fastest intervention you own. Also teach for home: call the provider for increa

Target SpO₂: 88–92% for a patient with COPD who retains CO₂ (corresponding to a PaO₂ of roughly 60–70 mmHg ). Start low — 1–3 L/min by nasal cannula or 24–28% by Venturi mask — and titrate. Note the contrast: for most other patients the goal is >94%; for COPD, more is not better.

entries.h: Why don't we aggressively administer oxygen to every COPD patient? ⭐
entries.t: Because in a chronic CO₂ retainer, flooding the patient with oxygen can make them stop breathing adequately and drive the CO₂ even higher — producing drowsiness, confusion, and respiratory arrest. Three mechanisms, and exams may ask for any of them: 1. Loss of the hypoxic drive (the classic nursing-exam answer). Normally a rising CO₂ is what tells the brain to breathe. In someone chronically hypercapnic, the brain has stopped responding to CO₂ and now uses a low oxygen level as its stimulus to breathe. Erase the low oxygen with high-flow O₂ and you erase the trigger — the respiratory rate and

Complete the flow: Start Trigger allergen, irritant, cold air, exercise, infection ➜ Blank 1 Airway inflammation — mast cells degranulate and release histamine, leukotrienes and prostaglandins → the bronchial lining swells ( mucosal edema ) ➜ Blank 2 Bronchoconstriction plus thick mucus plugging — the smooth muscle around the airways clamps down and the lumen fills with secretions ➜ Result Airflow obstruction worst on exhalation — but reversible Three things narrow the asthmatic airway: muscle spasm, swelling, and mucus. That is why one drug is never enough — a bronchodilator only fixes t

entries.h: Risk Factors — circle all that apply
entries.t: Allergies — ✅ Yes. Atopy (eczema, allergic rhinitis, food and environmental allergies) is the strongest predictor of childhood asthma — the same IgE-mediated response that causes hives in the skin causes bronchospasm in the lungs. Smoking — ✅ Yes — active and secondhand. Smoke inflames the airway, paralyzes the cilia, and makes the airway permanently more twitchy. Secondhand exposure in childhood is a major cause. GERD — ✅ Yes. Refluxed acid microaspirated into the airway irritates it directly, and acid in the esophagus also triggers a vagal reflex that causes bronchoconstriction. Asthma that

Potential Trigger Why It Matters Smoke A direct chemical irritant that inflames the airway lining and paralyzes the cilia , so the mucus the attack produces cannot be cleared. Tobacco, wood stoves, fireplaces and campfires all count. Teach: no smoking in the home or car, ever — airing the room out afterward does not remove the residue. Perfume Strong odors and volatile chemicals set off reflex bronchospasm in a hyperresponsive airway even though there is no allergy involved. The nerves in an asthmatic airway are hypersensitive — they react to the smell, not to an immune trigger. Same for scent

Wheezing — a high-pitched whistle, expiratory first , then inspiratory as obstruction worsens. Dyspnea — air hunger and a prolonged expiratory phase; the patient cannot get air out . Chest tightness — the sensation of the bronchial smooth muscle contracting and the chest staying hyperinflated. Patients often describe it as a band or a weight. Cough — often dry and worse at night or early morning. Cough-variant asthma may present with cough as the only symptom. Tachycardia — from hypoxia, from the sympathetic stress response, and from the beta-agonist rescue inhaler itself. A pulse rising along

Because air is being forced through airways that are too narrow, and the turbulence makes the airway walls vibrate — like air squeezing through a pinched straw. The narrowing comes from all three asthma changes at once: bronchospasm, mucosal swelling, and mucus. It is loudest on exhalation because airways naturally narrow further as the chest deflates and intrathoracic pressure rises. Critical: wheezing that suddenly disappears in a patient who is still struggling is NOT improvement. A "silent chest" means airflow has dropped too low to make any sound — that is impending respiratory arrest. Ge

To measure how much air the patient can move and how fast, and — the part that makes the diagnosis — to prove the obstruction is reversible . Spirometry is done, a bronchodilator is given, and spirometry is repeated: an increase in FEV₁ of at least 12% and 200 mL confirms asthma. A COPD patient's numbers barely budge. PFTs also establish a baseline, grade severity, and track response to therapy over time. A methacholine challenge can be used when spirometry is normal but asthma is still suspected.

entries.h: Peak flow meter — the home version she must know 📈
entries.t: Green zone: 80–100% of personal best — good control; continue the daily controller medication. Yellow zone: 50–79% — caution — the airway is narrowing. Use the rescue inhaler and follow the written asthma action plan; call the provider if the readings stay here. Red zone: below 50% — Medical emergency — use the rescue inhaler immediately and get emergency care. Teach: measure at the same time each day, stand up, take the best of three attempts, and establish "personal best" while well. A falling peak flow drops before the patient feels much worse — that early warning is the entire

A severe, prolonged asthma attack that does NOT respond to the usual rescue treatment — repeated bronchodilators and corticosteroids do not break it. The inflammation, bronchospasm and mucus plugging feed each other, so every breath adds more trapped air to a chest that is already full. It is the extreme end of an exacerbation, and it can develop over hours or over days.

Because the patient cannot exhale, so air stacks up until the lungs are so hyperinflated that ventilation essentially stops — and the respiratory muscles exhaust themselves trying. The chain: • Progressive air trapping → the lungs cannot empty → each breath moves less and less air. • Muscle fatigue → the work of breathing becomes unsustainable → ventilation collapses. • Severe hypoxemia + rising CO₂ → respiratory acidosis → confusion, then loss of consciousness. • Rising intrathoracic pressure → reduced venous return and cardiac output &ra

entries.h: ⚠️ The findings that mean "this patient is about to arrest"
entries.t: Silent chest — wheezing stops but the patient is still in distress. No airflow = no sound. This is the classic exam answer for "which finding requires immediate intervention." A "normal" or rising PaCO₂ on ABG. An asthmatic in distress should be hyperventilating and blowing OFF CO₂ — so a low PaCO₂ is expected. A PaCO₂ that has risen to normal means the patient is tiring and can no longer move air. Decreasing level of consciousness, drowsiness, or a patient who suddenly stops fighting. Calm is not improvement here. Inability to speak more than one or two words, cyanosis, bradycardia, or a fall

Oxygen — high-flow, humidified, titrated to keep SpO₂ >94% (asthma is not COPD — there is no 88–92% restriction here). Sit the patient upright. Albuterol — short-acting beta₂ agonist by nebulizer, often given continuously or back-to-back in status asthmaticus. Opens the airway within minutes. Ipratropium — anticholinergic added to albuterol in the emergency setting; it blocks the parasympathetic constriction pathway, so the two drugs open the airway by two different mechanisms and work better together than either alone. Corticosteroids — IV methylprednisolone or oral prednisone — given e

entries.h: Why is albuterol usually given first?
entries.t: Because it is the fastest — it relaxes the bronchial smooth muscle within about 5 minutes, so it directly relieves the bronchospasm that is choking the patient right now. There is a second reason that matters just as much: opening the airway first is what allows the other drugs and the oxygen to actually reach the lower airways. Give a steroid into a clamped-shut airway and much of it never gets there. Corticosteroids are essential but take hours; albuterol buys the time for them to work.

Step 1 Bronchodilator first albuterol (the rescue/SABA) — opens the airway ➜ Step 2 Wait about 5 minutes let the airway actually open ➜ Step 3 Then the corticosteroid it now travels deeper into the lung ➜ Step 4 Rinse mouth and spit after every steroid dose

entries.h: After using an inhaled corticosteroid, the patient should…
entries.t: Rinse the mouth with water and spit it out (and brush the teeth) after every dose.

Because steroid that settles on the mouth and throat suppresses the local immune defenses and lets Candida overgrow — oral thrush. Rinsing washes the leftover drug off the mucosa before it can do that. It also prevents hoarseness/dysphonia and a dry irritated throat. Spitting rather than swallowing keeps the extra drug from being absorbed systemically. Using a spacer with the MDI does the same job from the other end — it keeps large droplets from ever landing in the mouth and gets more drug into the lungs. MDI technique to teach: shake → exhale fully → seal lips (or use spacer) &rarr

Medication Type Example Purpose Short-Acting Beta Agonist Albuterol RESCUE. Stimulates beta₂ receptors on bronchial smooth muscle → rapid bronchodilation in about 5–15 minutes , lasting 4–6 hours. Used for an acute attack and 15–20 minutes before exercise . Not a daily controller. Side effects: tachycardia, tremor, jitteriness, nervousness, hypokalemia. Always the first inhaler when two are due. Anticholinergic Ipratropium Blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, which prevents the parasympathetic system from constricting the airway — and dries secretions. Slower on
Patient presents with: wheezing · tachypnea · short phrases · tripod position · chest tightness

All five — and two of them tell you it is severe . • Speaking in short phrases — ⭐ the strongest cue. How many words a patient can say in one breath is a bedside measure of how much air they can move. Full sentences = mild. Phrases = moderate–severe. Single words = severe . Cannot speak = emergency . • Tripod position — the patient is instinctively recruiting accessory muscles; nobody sits like that unless they need to. • Tachypnea — increased work of breathing and an attempt to compensate for hypoxemia. • Wheezing — confirms narrowed airways with air still moving. Re

entries.h: What is your priority nursing action?
entries.t: Stay with the patient, sit them upright, and administer oxygen — then give the prescribed short-acting bronchodilator (albuterol nebulizer). Priority is airway and breathing : the patient is hypoxic and obstructed right now, and oxygen plus a bronchodilator are the two interventions that reverse the immediate threat. Assessment and treatment happen simultaneously here — you do not complete a head-to-toe on a patient in respiratory distress. Never leave a patient in acute respiratory distress alone, and never lay them flat.

entries.h: What interventions should occur FIRST? (in order)
entries.t: STEP 1 Position upright — high-Fowler's or tripod. Free the diaphragm. Costs nothing, works instantly. ➜ STEP 2 Oxygen — titrate to SpO₂ >94% , continuous pulse oximetry. ➜ STEP 3 Albuterol nebulizer ± ipratropium — reverse the bronchospasm. ➜ STEP 4 Corticosteroid (IV/PO) — treat the swelling that the bronchodilator cannot reach. ➜ STEP 5 Reassess — breath sounds, speech, SpO₂, peak flow, mental status. Calm coaching, stay present. ➜ STEP 6 Escalate — if a silent chest, rising CO₂, or decreasing LOC appears, call rapid response and prepare for intubation. Once stable, teach: identify a

entries.h: 5 · Asthma vs COPD — the two that get confused ⭐
entries.t: Both obstruct airflow and both wheeze. The word that separates them is "reversible." Asthma COPD Core problem Reversible bronchospasm + inflammation of airways that are structurally normal between attacks Permanent structural damage — destroyed alveoli and/or chronically inflamed, mucus-filled airways Reversibility Reversible — FEV₁ improves ≥12% and 200 mL after a bronchodilator Not fully reversible — FEV₁/FVC stays <0.70 even after a bronchodilator Typical onset Childhood or young adulthood; often with allergies/eczema Usually after age 40, after decades of smoking or exposure Main cause

For every respiratory disorder ask… (this is the framework the course wants you to leave the module with) Ask… Lung cancer PE COPD Asthma What is happening in the lungs? A mass takes up space and obstructs A clot blocks perfusion — ventilation without blood flow Permanent obstruction → air trapping Reversible spasm + swelling + mucus What findings support it? Changed chronic cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, repeat pneumonia in one spot SUDDEN dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, anxiety, often clear lungs Barrel chest, pursed lips, prolonged expiration, chronic productive cough Expiratory

1. A client with severe asthma has been wheezing loudly for 30 minutes. The nurse reassesses and now hears almost no breath sounds, and the client can no longer speak. Which action is the priority? Document that the wheezing has resolved and continue to monitor Call the rapid response team and prepare for intubation Encourage pursed-lip breathing and offer reassurance Recheck the peak flow reading Show the answer Answer: 2 — call rapid response and prepare for intubation. A silent chest in a client who is still in distress means airflow has dropped below the level that can generate any sound.

1. COPD SpO₂ target is 88–92%. Higher saturations can knock out the hypoxic drive, worsen V/Q mismatch and raise CO₂. But never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient — give it controlled and titrated. If a COPD patient gets sleepy and calm, suspect CO₂ narcosis, not improvement. 2. COPD is an exhalation problem. Air trapping → barrel chest, flattened diaphragm, hypercapnia, blebs. Pursed-lip breathing splints the airways open so the lungs can empty — in 2 counts through the nose, out 4 counts through pursed lips. 3. A silent chest in an asthmatic is an emergency. No wheeze + still

Answer those three in order and the ABG interprets itself. 🙈 Hide answers — quiz me Every highlighted answer was a blank in the handout. 1 · Rules Before You Start 2 · Normal Values ⭐ 3 · ROME + The 5 Steps 4 · Tic-Tac-Toe Grid 5 · Compensation 6 · Causes Cheat Sheet 7 · What the Patient Looks Like 8 · Questions 1–7 9 · Questions 8–14 10 · Questions 15–20 🚨 The Two Killers in This Set ⭐ Must not forget
This is the handout's own opening list. Ask these five questions in this order , every time, before you look at the answer choices.

Is the pH acidic or alkalotic? pH < 7.35 = acidosis , pH > 7.45 = alkalosis . If the pH is inside 7.35–7.45, it is normal — but still lean it: 7.35–7.39 is the acid half, 7.41–7.45 is the alkaline half. Is the problem respiratory or metabolic? Look at which value matches the pH . CO₂ is the lung value — if pH and CO₂ move in opposite directions it is respiratory. HCO₃ is the kidney value — if pH and HCO₃ move in the same direction it is metabolic. (ROME) What caused it? Respiratory problems = a ventilation problem (COPD, opioids, sedation, pneumonia → acidosis; anxiety,

You cannot interpret an ABG you cannot compare. Memorize these six lines; three of them do 90% of the work. pH = 7.35 – 7.45 (no units — it is a log scale) PaCO₂ = 35 – 45 mm Hg — the LUNG number (this is an acid) HCO₃ (bicarbonate) = 22 – 26 mEq/L — the KIDNEY number (this is a base) PaO₂ = 80 – 100 mm Hg (oxygenation — separate question from acid-base) SaO₂ = 95 – 100% (88–92% is an acceptable target in chronic CO₂ retainers) Base excess = −2 to +2 mEq/L (negative = acid load, positive = base load)

entries.h: Which way does each number point?
entries.t: Value Below normal means… Above normal means… pH < 7.35 = ACIDOSIS > 7.45 = ALKALOSIS CO₂ (acid) < 35 = blowing acid off → alkalotic > 45 = holding acid in → acidotic HCO₃ (base) < 22 = lost base → acidotic > 26 = extra base → alkalotic CO₂ is backwards — a HIGH CO₂ means a LOW pH. Because CO₂ + water becomes carbonic acid; more CO₂ = more acid. HCO₃ is not backwards: high bicarb, high pH.

R espiratory O pposite — pH and CO₂ move in opposite directions. pH ↓ with CO₂ ↑ = respiratory acidosis. pH ↑ with CO₂ ↓ = respiratory alkalosis. M etabolic E qual — pH and HCO₃ move in the same direction. pH ↓ with HCO₃ ↓ = metabolic acidosis. pH ↑ with HCO₃ ↑ = metabolic alkalosis. 💡 If you only remember one thing: find the value that matches the pH's direction. That value names the problem. The other value is either normal or compensating.

Step 1 · pH Acid or base? <7.35 acidosis · >7.45 alkalosis · in range = look for compensation ➜ Step 2 · CO₂ Lung value. Opposite the pH? → RESPIRATORY ➜ Step 3 · HCO₃ Kidney value. Same way as the pH? → METABOLIC ➜ Step 4 · Compensation Other value normal = none · abnormal + pH still off = partial · abnormal + pH normal = full ➜ Step 5 · Patient Cause? Airway/breathing OK? Potassium? THAT is the test question. Naming format the exam wants: [uncompensated / partially compensated / fully compensated] + [respiratory / metabolic] + [acidosis / alkalosis] . Say all three parts out loud a

Draw three columns. Drop each number into the column it belongs to. Whatever lands in the same column as the pH is the primary problem. Put it here… ACID column NORMAL column BASE column pH < 7.35 7.35 – 7.45 > 7.45 CO₂ (mm Hg) > 45 35 – 45 < 35 HCO₃ (mEq/L) < 22 22 – 26 > 26

entries.h: How to read your own grid
entries.t: pH + CO₂ in the same column → respiratory problem, named by the pH's column (acid column = acidosis) pH + HCO₃ in the same column → metabolic problem, named by the pH's column The third value still sitting in the NORMAL column → uncompensated — the other system has not started helping yet Both CO₂ and HCO₃ out of the normal column, pH still abnormal → partially compensated Both CO₂ and HCO₃ out of the normal column, pH back inside 7.35–7.45 → fully compensated — then use the 7.40 split to say which one was primary 💡 The 7.40 split (only for a normal pH): 7.35&nda

The two systems cover for each other. Whichever one is not broken is the one doing the compensating. System Compensates for How Speed 🫁 Lungs (CO₂) Metabolic problems Change rate & depth — blow off CO₂ in acidosis, hold CO₂ in alkalosis Minutes — fast, but incomplete 🫘 Kidneys (HCO₃) Respiratory problems Retain or dump bicarbonate and excrete H⁺ Hours to 2–3 days — slow, but far more complete

State pH CO₂ & HCO₃ Read it as Uncompensated Abnormal One abnormal, one normal Brand new — help hasn't arrived Partially compensated Still abnormal Both abnormal Help is on the way but losing Fully compensated NORMAL Both abnormal Chronic — the body caught up Normal pH + two abnormal values = fully compensated. It is never "normal ABG." Never treat the compensation. Kussmaul breathing in DKA and a fast rate in metabolic acidosis are the patient's rescue — sedating or slowing that breathing removes the only thing holding the pH up.

Most of the questions below are really "name the cause." Learn these four columns and you can answer without an ABG at all. Imbalance Mechanism Classic causes Respiratory acidosis ↑CO₂, ↓pH HYPOventilation — not blowing CO₂ off COPD · opioids / sedatives / anesthesia · pneumonia, atelectasis · chest trauma, flail chest · neuromuscular disease (MG, Guillain-Barré) · obesity hypoventilation, OSA · airway obstruction · post-op splinting Respiratory alkalosis ↓CO₂, ↑pH HYPERventilation — blowing too much CO₂ off Anxiety / panic · pain · fever · early sepsis · pulmonary e

entries.h: Two shortcuts that cover most items
entries.t: The belly-button rule: Fluid lost from above the belly button (vomiting, NG suction) is acid → metabolic ALKALOSIS . Fluid lost from below (diarrhea, ileostomy, fistula) is bicarbonate-rich → metabolic ACIDOSIS . The breathing rule: If the question describes slow or shallow breathing, the answer is respiratory acidosis . If it describes fast, deep, or panicked breathing as the problem , it is respiratory alkalosis . If fast and deep breathing is the body's response to something else, it is compensation for metabolic acidosis .

entries.h: 7 · What the Patient Actually Looks Like 👁️
entries.t: The exam rarely hands you an ABG in the clinical items — it hands you a patient. Acidosis sedates. Alkalosis irritates. ACIDOSIS — CNS depression ALKALOSIS — CNS excitement Neuro Headache, drowsy, confused, lethargic → coma Anxious, lightheaded, dizzy, seizures Neuromuscular Weakness, flaccid, hyporeflexia Tingling: circumoral, fingers, toes · twitching, tetany, carpopedal spasm, +Chvostek/Trousseau Cardiac Hyperkalemia → peaked T waves, wide QRS, bradycardia, VF Hypokalemia → flat T waves, U waves, PVCs; tachycardia Respiratory Kussmaul (deep, rapid, labored) if metabolic; slow

Cover the reveal. Write your three-part name (compensation + system + acid/base) before you tap. Q1. A patient has the following ABG results: pH 7.31 · CO₂ 52 · HCO₃ 24. What acid-base imbalance is present? Metabolic acidosis Respiratory acidosis Respiratory alkalosis Metabolic alkalosis Show the answer Answer: B — respiratory acidosis (uncompensated). Reading the numbers: pH 7.31 → below 7.35 → acidosis . CO₂ 52 → above 45 → acidic , and it moved opposite the pH. R espiratory O pposite → this is the primary problem. HCO₃ 24 → inside 22–26 → normal , so

Q8. True or False: Kussmaul respirations are commonly seen in metabolic acidosis. TRUE FALSE Show the answer Answer: TRUE. Why: Kussmaul respirations are deep, rapid, labored breaths. When the pH falls, chemoreceptors drive the lungs to blow off CO₂ (carbonic acid) to pull the pH back up. It is the textbook finding in DKA and in severe metabolic acidosis of any cause. The exam trap: Kussmaul breathing is compensation, not the emergency . Never give a sedative or try to slow that breathing. Fix the acidosis (insulin, fluids, perfusion) and the breathing settles on its own. Q9. A nurse reviews t

Q15. A patient has: pH 7.32 · CO₂ 29 · HCO₃ 18. What is the BEST interpretation? Fully compensated metabolic acidosis Partially compensated metabolic acidosis Respiratory alkalosis Uncompensated respiratory acidosis Show the answer Answer: B — partially compensated metabolic acidosis. Reading the numbers: pH 7.32 → below 7.35 → acidosis , and still abnormal. HCO₃ 18 → below 22 → acidic , same direction as the pH → metabolic is the primary problem (ME). CO₂ 29 → below 35 → alkalotic, which does not match the pH — so it is not causing the problem, it is fixing

entries.h: 11 · The Two Killers Hidden in This Set 🚨
entries.t: Twenty questions, two of them are actually emergencies. These are the ones that become "which patient first" items.

entries.h: 🚨 Killer 1 — the falling respiratory rate (Q10, Q16)
entries.t: Trigger: RR under 10–12 after an opioid, benzodiazepine, or anesthesia — especially with difficulty arousing Why it kills: CO₂ accumulates within minutes and the pH crashes; the kidneys cannot compensate for days, so there is no backup system . Hypoxia and arrest follow. Do: Stimulate → open the airway → oxygen → bag-valve-mask ventilation if the rate keeps falling → hold the opioid → naloxone per protocol → keep monitoring for re-sedation Never leave a sedated patient with a falling respiratory rate to "check on them later."

entries.h: 🚨 Killer 2 — potassium riding with the pH (Q18)
entries.t: Rule: Acidosis → hyperkalemia (K⁺ leaves the cell). Alkalosis → hypokalemia (K⁺ enters the cell). The number to fear: K⁺ above 5.0 mEq/L , and urgently above 6.0 — peaked T waves, widening QRS, then VF or asystole Do first: Cardiac monitor and 12-lead ECG, then IV calcium gluconate to stabilize the myocardium (it does not lower the potassium — it buys time) , then insulin with dextrose to shift it, then a binder or dialysis to remove it ⚠️ Also on the danger list: lethargy in a COPD patient (Q6) — that is CO₂ narcosis, an early sign of respiratory failure, not a patient finally resti

If she reads nothing else the morning of the exam, she reads this. 1. pH 7.35–7.45 · CO₂ 35–45 mm Hg · HCO₃ 22–26 mEq/L . Nothing else can be interpreted until these three are memorized. 2. ROME. Respiratory = pH and CO₂ Opposite . Metabolic = pH and HCO₃ Equal . Whichever value matches the pH's direction names the disorder. 3. CO₂ is an acid, HCO₃ is a base. High CO₂ = low pH. High bicarb = high pH. 4. Lungs are fast (minutes), kidneys are slow (2–3 days). Lungs compensate for metabolic problems; kidneys compensate for respiratory ones. 5. Normal pH + two abnormal valu

entries.h: 🚨 What Kills First — The Priority Order
entries.t: When two patients both have an abnormal electrolyte, this is how you choose. Assess the one whose organ can stop in the next few minutes. 1 — RHYTHM Potassium or calcium abnormality WITH ECG changes. Widened QRS, peaked T waves, torsades. This patient arrests first — nothing outranks it. ➜ 2 — AIRWAY / BREATHING Hypermagnesemia with absent reflexes and shallow respirations , or hypocalcemia with stridor/laryngospasm . The drive to breathe or the airway itself is going. ➜ 3 — BRAIN Severe sodium change with neuro symptoms — Na <120 with confusion, or a seizing patient. Cerebral edema → her

1. A patient has a sodium level of 124 mEq/L. Which assessment finding is MOST concerning? Dry skin Confusion Constipation Bradycardia Show the answer Answer: 2 — confusion. Sodium 124 mEq/L is well below 135. Water follows the low sodium into the brain cells, they swell, and intracranial pressure rises — so confusion is the first sign that the brain is in trouble and the last warning before seizures and coma. Why the others are wrong: 1. Dry skin points to fluid volume deficit or high sodium, not low, and dry skin never killed anyone. 3. Constipation belongs to hypercalcemia and hypokalemia,

6. A patient with sodium 154 mEq/L is MOST likely to exhibit: Seizures from cerebral edema Dry mucous membranes and thirst Tetany Bounding pulses Show the answer Answer: 2 — dry mucous membranes and thirst. Sodium 154 mEq/L pulls water out of the cells into the bloodstream, so the cells are dehydrated. Thirst is the body's first defense , and dry sticky mucous membranes are the most reliable bedside sign of a true water deficit. Why the others are wrong: 1. Cerebral edema is a hypo natremia problem — cells swell when sodium is low. High sodium shrinks brain cells. (Hypernatremia can still seiz

11. True or False: Hyperkalemia can cause life-threatening dysrhythmias. True False Show the answer Answer: TRUE. Hyperkalemia is the electrolyte most likely to kill your patient today. Excess extracellular potassium keeps cardiac cells partially depolarized so they cannot reset, which produces peaked T waves, a widening QRS, then ventricular fibrillation or asystole. Continuous cardiac monitoring is non-negotiable. Why "false" is wrong: nothing about hyperkalemia is benign at high levels — and the danger does not track neatly with the number. A patient at 6.0 with a wide QRS is sicker than a

16. A patient with severe vomiting is MOST at risk for: Hyperkalemia Hypokalemia Hypermagnesemia Hypernatremia Show the answer Answer: 2 — hypokalemia. Vomiting loses potassium two ways: directly in the gastric fluid, and indirectly through the metabolic alkalosis it creates . Losing acid raises the pH, and potassium shifts into the cells in exchange for hydrogen ions — so the serum level falls even further. The same is true of continuous NG suction. Why the others are wrong: 1. Hyperkalemia goes with acid osis and kidney failure, not with losing acid out the top. 3. Hypermagnesemia requires r

21. A patient with hyponatremia is becoming increasingly confused. Which IV fluid would the nurse anticipate? 0.45% NS D5W 3% saline Sterile water Show the answer Answer: 3 — 3% saline. This is symptomatic hyponatremia: the confusion means the brain is already swelling. Hypertonic saline raises serum osmolality so water is pulled back out of the brain cells. Give it on an infusion pump , recheck sodium frequently, and never correct sodium faster than about 8–12 mEq/L in 24 hours — too-fast correction causes osmotic demyelination. Why the others are wrong: 1. 0.45% NS is hypotonic — it dr
