entries.h: Unit 1 · The Kidneys: Why Should We Care? 🫘
entries.t: Before you learn the diseases — the kidneys have ONE job: keep the body in balance. The six jobs. Every renal disease in this module is one of these six jobs failing. Learn the six, and the signs and symptoms write themselves. Kidney function What happens if the kidneys stop doing it What you'd see in your patient Filter wastes Urea, creatinine and other nitrogenous wastes stay in the blood — uremia . BUN and creatinine climb, GFR falls. Confusion, lethargy, nausea, metallic taste, itching, uremic breath (fetor), later pericarditis Remove excess fluid Water is retained in the vascular space &r

Your patient has crackles, +3 edema, weight gain, and urine output of 80 mL today. You don't know the diagnosis yet. What kidney function has failed? Fluid removal. The kidney is not excreting water, so volume is being held in the vascular space and pushed into the interstitium and the lungs. What assessment finding worries you the most? The crackles — that is fluid in the alveoli, which is an airway/breathing problem. Why? Edema and weight gain are uncomfortable; pulmonary edema kills. ABCs put oxygenation ahead of everything else, so crackles + 80 mL of urine in a day means this patient is h
Don't memorize diseases. Recognize patterns. Finish the arrows.

Start Kidneys cannot filter blood ➜ Then BUN rises (>20 mg/dL) ➜ Then Creatinine rises (>1.3 mg/dL) ➜ Then Waste products accumulate in the blood ➜ Result Patient becomes uremic — confused, nauseated, itchy, lethargic

Start Kidneys cannot remove water ➜ Then Fluid is retained / overload develops ➜ Then Blood pressure increases ➜ Then Lungs fill with fluid ➜ Result Patient develops pulmonary edema — crackles, dyspnea, falling SpO₂, frothy sputum

Start Kidneys cannot remove potassium ➜ Then Potassium rises — hyperkalemia ➜ Then Heart becomes electrically irritable and unstable ➜ Result ECG may show tall peaked T waves → flat/absent P waves → widened QRS → VF or asystole

entries.h: ⛔ Stop & Think — which problem could kill your patient FIRST?
entries.t: ☐ Elevated BUN — ❌ Makes the patient feel awful (nausea, confusion) but does not stop the heart today. ☐ Elevated creatinine — ❌ Tells you how injured the kidney is. It is a marker, not the killer. ☐ Hyperkalemia — ✅ THIS ONE. Potassium changes cardiac membrane excitability — lethal dysrhythmias can occur within minutes. ☐ Anemia — ❌ Chronic and treatable with epoetin alfa and iron; it is a "weeks" problem, not a "minutes" problem. Renal rule #1: the lab that kills first is potassium. Mini NCLEX — A client with acute kidney injury develops peaked T waves on telemetry. Which action has the high
Look only at the assessment. Can you figure out what's happening?

entries.h: Patient #1 — 82 y/o, vomiting 4 days, BP 82/46, HR 124, UOP 15 mL/hr, BUN ↑, Cr ↑, K⁺ 5.0
entries.t: ☐ Prerenal — ✅ Prerenal AKI. Four days of vomiting = volume loss → hypotension → the kidney is not being perfused . ☐ Intrarenal — ❌ Nothing here is toxic to or inflaming the kidney tissue itself. ☐ Postrenal — ❌ No obstruction: no distended bladder, no BPH history, no stone. Evidence? Hypotension (82/46) + tachycardia (124, compensating) + dry losses + oliguria (15 mL/hr is well under 0.5 mL/kg/hr). Classic prerenal picture: BUN rises out of proportion to creatinine — a BUN:creatinine ratio above about 20:1 , because the slow tubular flow lets urea be reabsorbed.

entries.h: Patient #2 — Received IV contrast yesterday; creatinine doubled overnight; urine output down
entries.t: Diagnosis? Intrarenal AKI — contrast-induced nephropathy / acute tubular necrosis (ATN) Why? Iodinated contrast is directly toxic to the tubular cells and causes renal vasoconstriction, so the damage is inside the kidney. It typically shows up 24–72 hours after the scan. Prevention: hydrate with IV isotonic fluid before and after, use the smallest dye load, and hold nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs, aminoglycosides and metformin around the study.

entries.h: Patient #3 — History of BPH, distended bladder, cannot urinate, pain 8/10
entries.t: Diagnosis? Postrenal AKI from acute urinary retention caused by the enlarged prostate obstructing the urethra What intervention comes FIRST? Relieve the obstruction — bladder scan and then insert a urinary catheter per order to drain the bladder. Nothing else works until urine can leave; the back-pressure is what is destroying the kidney, and draining it also fixes the 8/10 pain. ⚠️ After you drain: Watch for post-obstructive diuresis — huge urine volumes over the next hours with hypotension, hypokalemia and hyponatremia. Monitor I&O, BP and electrolytes closely. Notice: you haven't memorized

entries.h: Unit 4 · Renal Diagnostics 🧪 — What Are the Kidneys Trying to Tell You?
entries.t: The kidney is a coffee filter. If the filter clogs, the waste doesn't leave — it stays in the bloodstream. That is why kidney disease causes abnormal labs.

Lab (normal) What does it measure? A HIGH value usually means… Why? BUN 10–20 mg/dL Urea nitrogen — the nitrogen waste from protein breakdown Reduced filtration or a non-renal cause Rises with dehydration, GI bleeding, high protein intake, steroids, catabolism — so a high BUN alone does not prove kidney disease. Falls with fluid overload and liver failure. Creatinine 0.6–1.2 mg/dL (women slightly lower) Waste from muscle metabolism, produced at a steady rate and cleared almost entirely by the kidney The kidney is no longer filtering effectively Because production is constant, a ris

Creatinine is the BEST indicator of kidney function. Unlike BUN, it is barely affected by hydration status, diet, or GI bleeding — it comes from muscle at a steady rate, so a rise means the filter has failed.

entries.h: Let's Practice — BUN 42, Creatinine 3.1, GFR 18, K⁺ 6.2
entries.t: What concerns you FIRST? The potassium of 6.2 mEq/L. Why? It is the only value on that list that can cause a fatal dysrhythmia in the next few minutes. Get a 12-lead/telemetry, look for peaked T waves, and expect calcium gluconate, insulin + dextrose, and a plan for removal (binder or dialysis). The GFR of 18 tells you this is stage 4–5 disease — important, but not the emergency.

entries.h: ⛔ Stop and Think — which value means immediate risk of sudden death?
entries.t: ☐ BUN — ❌ Reflects waste build-up and hydration; causes symptoms, not arrest. ☐ Creatinine — ❌ Best measure of function , but a high number does not itself stop the heart. ☐ Potassium — ✅ Yes. Hyperkalemia depolarizes the cardiac membrane → peaked T waves, wide QRS, VF/asystole. ☐ GFR — ❌ Stages the disease and guides drug dosing; a chronic number, not an acute threat. NCLEX Corner — A nurse receives four laboratory reports. Which result requires immediate intervention? Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL Potassium 6.4 mEq/L BUN 45 mg/dL GFR 32 mL/min Show the answer B — Potassium 6.4 mEq/L. Because it

entries.h: Clinical Judgment — "The patient's creatinine doubled overnight." What questions pop into your head?
entries.t: 1. Is the patient making urine? How many mL in the last hour and the last 24 hours? 2. What did we do to them? Any IV contrast, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, ACE inhibitors, or a hypotensive episode in the last 48 hours? 3. What is the potassium (and the ECG)? Doubling creatinine means K⁺ and acid are being retained too. 4. Is it volume? What are the BP, HR, weight, and I&O trend — are they dry (prerenal) or overloaded? 5. Could this be obstruction? Bladder scan — a distended bladder is fixable in five minutes. 💬 Ask Claire: "I am studying renal laboratory values. Instead of making me m
Picture where the infection is. The higher the infection travels, the sicker the patient becomes.

entries.h: Follow the Infection — complete the pathway
entries.t: Start Outside world ➜ 1 Urethra (urethritis) ➜ 2 Bladder (cystitis) ➜ 3 Ureters (ureteritis) ➜ 4 Kidneys (pyelonephritis) Why women get more UTIs: a much shorter urethra sitting closer to the rectum, so E. coli — the cause of ~80–90% of UTIs — has a shorter trip.

Disorder Location Usually serious? Urethritis Urethra — the lowest point of the tract No — burning and discharge; treated outpatient Cystitis Bladder (lower UTI) Usually no — local symptoms, afebrile, oral antibiotics Pyelonephritis Kidney — renal pelvis and parenchyma (upper UTI) YES — systemic illness, can scar the kidney and progress to urosepsis; often needs IV antibiotics and admission

entries.h: Pattern Recognition — lower UTI vs. kidney infection
entries.t: Finding Lower UTI (cystitis) Kidney infection (pyelonephritis) Burning with urination ✅ hallmark ✅ often present too Frequency ✅ ✅ Urgency ✅ ✅ Fever ❌ usually afebrile ✅ high fever — the tip-off that it went upstairs Chills ❌ ✅ shaking chills / rigors Flank pain / CVA tenderness ❌ suprapubic pressure instead ✅ the single best discriminator Nausea / vomiting ❌ ✅ systemic illness Confusion (older adult) ✅ new confusion may be the ONLY sign of any UTI in an older adult ✅ and it raises your suspicion for sepsis

entries.h: 🩺 Think Like the Nurse — "My back really hurts," right over the costovertebral angle
entries.t: Why does this matter? CVA tenderness means the pain is over the kidney, not the bladder. The infection has ascended — think pyelonephritis, which is a systemic infection that can scar the kidney and seed the bloodstream. ⛔ What assessment should you perform next? Take a full set of vital signs — temperature, HR, BP, RR and mental status — looking for the sepsis picture (fever, HR >100, SBP <100, confusion). Then percuss the CVA gently and check the urine.

entries.h: Clinical Case — Mrs. Wilson, 79, "she just isn't acting like herself"
entries.t: Temp 100.9°F · confused · weak · urinary frequency · BP 100/62 · HR 112 Q1 — What should the nurse suspect FIRST? A urinary tract infection, likely already ascending — and possible early urosepsis. Get a urinalysis with culture, blood cultures, and vitals. Q2 — Why is this different from a younger adult? Older adults often do not mount the classic burning/frequency picture or a high fever. Their presenting sign is a change in mental status — new confusion, falls, incontinence, decreased appetite, or generalized weakness. A "normal" temperature can still be a fever for them because their baseli

Cloudy · nitrites positive · leukocyte esterase positive · WBC elevated · bacteria present · SG 1.025 · trace protein Most likely diagnosis? Bacterial urinary tract infection. Positive nitrites = gram-negative bacteria (usually E. coli ) converting dietary nitrate; positive leukocyte esterase + WBCs = the inflammatory response. Would you expect antibiotics? YES / NO YES — this is a symptomatic bacterial infection. Culture first, then antibiotics. Note SG 1.025 is normal-to-concentrated (normal 1.005–1.030) and trace protein is not alarming here.

1 — Assess pain (assessment before intervention; also tells you whether this is bladder or flank pain) 2 — Obtain urine culture (must be collected BEFORE the first antibiotic dose) 3 — Administer prescribed antibiotic (treat the infection promptly once the specimen is in hand) 4 — Encourage oral fluids (flushes bacteria; supportive, not urgent) 5 — Teach front-to-back wiping (prevention/teaching is always last when someone is acutely ill) Why must the culture come before antibiotics? Even one dose can suppress bacterial growth and give a false-negative culture. Without a positive culture and s

Don't stop at "this patient has a UTI." Ask: How sick are they? Has it spread upward? Could this become sepsis? And — the one that matters — what finding would make me call the provider immediately? Answer: fever with hypotension, tachycardia, rising lactate, or new confusion.
Don't memorize the types — meet the patients. For each one ask: "Why is this patient leaking urine?"

entries.h: Patient A — 42 y/o woman: "Every time I laugh, sneeze, or cough, I leak a little."
entries.t: Type? Stress incontinence WHY? Weak pelvic floor muscles and a weak urethral sphincter, usually after childbirth, aging, or estrogen loss. A cough spikes intra-abdominal pressure above what the sphincter can hold, so a small amount escapes. The bladder itself is normal. First-line treatment? Pelvic floor muscle (Kegel) exercises — plus weight loss, avoiding caffeine/alcohol, and timed voiding. Surgery (sling) and pessaries come later.

entries.h: Patient B — 73 y/o: "When I feel like I have to go, I have about 10 seconds."
entries.t: Type? Urge incontinence (overactive bladder) What is happening inside the bladder? The detrusor muscle contracts involuntarily and too early, before the bladder is actually full — so the urge is sudden, intense, and unstoppable. Nursing intervention? Bladder retraining with a timed voiding schedule, gradually lengthening the interval; cut caffeine, alcohol and artificial sweeteners; keep a path to the toilet clear; anticholinergics such as oxybutynin or tolterodine, or mirabegron, if prescribed.

entries.h: Patient C — 82 y/o man with BPH: "I always feel full." Dribbles all day. Bladder scan 850 mL.
entries.t: Type? Overflow incontinence Why? The enlarged prostate obstructs outflow. The bladder over-distends, pressure inside exceeds sphincter resistance, and urine dribbles out over the top — while 850 mL stays behind. Leaking urine does NOT mean the bladder is empty. Priority nursing action? Relieve the retention — bladder scan (done: 850 mL) then catheterize per order. Because that retained volume causes back-pressure → hydronephrosis → postrenal AKI, plus a high infection risk.

entries.h: Patient D — spinal cord injury; bladder empties without warning; no control
entries.t: Type? Reflex incontinence — a neurogenic bladder Why? The spinal cord lesion cuts the communication between bladder and brain. The bladder fills and the reflex arc fires a detrusor contraction at a set volume, with no sensation and no voluntary control. Managed with a scheduled program of intermittent catheterization.

entries.h: Patient E — severe arthritis; can't unbutton pants fast enough
entries.t: Is the bladder working normally? YES / NO YES. The urinary system is intact. Then why is the patient incontinent? This is functional incontinence — a mobility, dexterity, cognition or environment problem, not a bladder problem. Fix the environment: elastic waistbands and Velcro, a bedside commode, a call light within reach, good lighting, clear pathways, and scheduled toileting.

entries.h: Patient F — new incontinence after starting a diuretic; resolves when the drug is adjusted
entries.t: Type? Transient (temporary) incontinence — caused by a reversible trigger. Remember DIAPPERS : Delirium, Infection, Atrophic vaginitis, Pharmaceuticals, Psychological, Excess urine output, Restricted mobility, Stool impaction. 🩺 Think Like a Nurse — Which patient requires the nurse's attention FIRST? Stress incontinence Overflow incontinence with bladder distention Functional incontinence Urge incontinence Show the answer B — Overflow incontinence with bladder distention. Because this one is causing organ damage right now: retained urine raises pressure back up the ureters → hydronephrosi

entries.h: ⛔ Stop & Think — no void in 10 hours, palpable bladder, leaking urine
entries.t: Should the nurse assume the bladder is empty? YES / NO NO. Why? Leaking with a palpable bladder is the classic picture of overflow — the bladder is so full it is spilling. Scan it. If a large residual is present, catheterize per order. Assuming "she's voiding, she's fine" is how retention becomes hydronephrosis. 💡 Clinical Pearl: Overflow incontinence fools students. Leaking urine sometimes means the bladder is too full, not empty. 💬 Ask Claire: "Give me six patient scenarios with different types of urinary incontinence. Do not tell me the diagnosis. Make me identify the type, explain the path

Lots of urinary problems cause blood in the urine. Bladder cancer is different because of HOW the blood shows up. The classic sign is gross, painless, intermittent hematuria — visibly bloody urine with no burning, no colic, no fever Why is this finding concerning? Painless bleeding means nothing is inflamed, obstructed, or spasming — so infection and stones do not explain it. Untreated bladder cancer keeps growing while the patient feels fine, and the bleeding is intermittent , so people talk themselves out of getting checked when it clears up.

"My urine has blood in it, but it doesn't hurt." The question that should come to mind: "Does this patient smoke, or have they ever?" — and then: painless hematuria in an adult is bladder cancer until proven otherwise. It needs cystoscopy, not reassurance.

Risk factor Why does it increase risk? Cigarette smoking The #1 modifiable risk factor. Carcinogens from tobacco are absorbed, filtered by the kidney, and then sit in contact with the bladder lining while urine is stored — a chemical bath on the urothelium. Smokers have roughly 2–4× the risk. Older age Decades of accumulated carcinogen exposure plus age-related DNA repair decline. Most cases are diagnosed after age 55. Male sex Men are diagnosed about 3–4× more often — historically higher smoking and industrial-chemical exposure, plus hormonal differences in the urothel

Test Purpose Urinalysis May detect blood in the urine — often microscopic hematuria; a screening clue, never the diagnosis CT scan Evaluates spread of disease — staging: depth of invasion, nodes, metastasis Cystoscopy Looks directly inside the bladder — the key test; the scope both visualizes and removes tissue Biopsy Confirms the diagnosis — only tissue proves cancer and its grade After cystoscopy, teach: pink-tinged urine and mild burning are expected for a day or two; increase fluids; report bright red bleeding with clots, inability to void, fever, or worsening pain. Priority Question — A p
After the bladder comes out, urine still has to leave the body. The surgeon builds a new road.

Start Kidney ➜ 1 Ureters ➜ 2 Ileal conduit — a short segment of ileum used as a pipe ➜ 3 Stoma on the abdominal wall ➜ End Collection pouch Key point: an ileal conduit is incontinent and continuous — there is no storage and no sphincter, so urine drains constantly and the pouch is worn 24/7. Expect mucus in the urine; that is normal because the conduit is made of bowel.

entries.h: What Does the Nurse Assess? — circle all that apply
entries.t: Stoma color — ✅ the single most important assessment — it tells you whether the tissue is perfused Skin integrity — ✅ alkaline urine excoriates peristomal skin quickly Urine output — ✅ must be at least ~30 mL/hr; no output = obstruction or hypovolemia Pulse quality — ❌ not a stoma assessment (still part of a general post-op check, just not part of this) Pouch seal — ✅ a leaking seal means skin breakdown and odor within hours Edema around stoma — ✅ mild edema is expected for the first few days; increasing edema is not

entries.h: Healthy or Not? — a stoma should be…
entries.t: ☐ Pale — ❌ suggests anemia or poor perfusion ☐ Black — ❌ necrosis — a surgical emergency ☐ Moist and pink/red — ✅ correct — looks like the inside of your cheek, beefy red and shiny ☐ Dry — ❌ a healthy stoma is always moist; dryness signals compromise

entries.h: 🚨 Critical Thinking — the stoma suddenly turns dark purple
entries.t: Priority concern? Impaired blood supply to the stoma — ischemia progressing toward necrosis. Dusky/purple → black means the tissue is dying and the patient needs surgical revision. What should you do FIRST? Notify the surgeon immediately. Ischemic bowel does not recover on its own and cannot be fixed at the bedside. Meanwhile, remove any constricting pouch/belt, do not apply heat or massage, keep the patient NPO in case of a return to the OR, and document the exact color and time.

1 Bladder removed (cystectomy) ➜ 2 Need another way to eliminate urine ➜ 3 Procedure: ileal conduit (incontinent), or a continent reservoir such as a Kock/Indiana pouch that the patient catheterizes, or a neobladder ➜ 4 Nursing priorities: stoma color & perfusion, urine output ≥30 mL/hr, peristomal skin protection and a good pouch seal, infection prevention, fluid intake ~2–3 L/day, and body-image support NCLEX Priority — One day after creation of an ileal conduit, which finding requires immediate intervention? Pink stoma Yellow urine draining Dark purple stoma Mild edema around the stom

entries.h: 🩺 End-of-Section Reflection — What Have You Learned? ⭐
entries.t: Without looking back — biggest clue, and the thing you are most worried about. Disorder Biggest clue Priority nursing concern Stress incontinence Leaks with cough, laugh, sneeze, lifting Skin breakdown and social withdrawal — teach pelvic floor exercises; it is not an emergency Overflow incontinence Constant dribbling with a distended, palpable bladder and a large post-void residual Urinary retention → hydronephrosis and postrenal AKI — scan and drain Neurogenic bladder Neuro injury (SCI, MS, stroke) with emptying the patient cannot feel or control Safe, scheduled emptying — intermittent

entries.h: Clinical Judgment — "I have blood in my urine." Five questions before you call the provider
entries.t: 1. Does it hurt? Painless points toward cancer; colicky flank pain points toward a stone; burning points toward infection. 2. When did it start, and is it every void or just at the beginning/end of the stream? Blood throughout suggests a kidney or bladder source. 3. What does it look like — bright red, pink, clots, or cola-colored? Cola/tea colored with edema and hypertension = glomerulonephritis, not bleeding. 4. What else is going on — fever, chills, flank pain, weight loss, trouble voiding? 5. What is your history? Smoking, chemical exposure, anticoagulants, recent procedure or catheter, tr

Nursing isn't recognizing a disease name. It is asking: Why is this happening? What is the priority? What complication am I trying to prevent? What assessment tells me my patient is getting worse? Answer those four and you are thinking like a nurse — which is exactly what NCLEX tests.

entries.h: Unit 9 · Glomerulonephritis — When the Filter Becomes Inflamed 🔥
entries.t: Normally: blood enters, waste leaves, protein stays, red cells stay. Now the filter develops tiny holes because it is inflamed.

entries.h: What can now leak through? — circle all that apply
entries.t: □ Water — Water always crosses the filter — that is normal filtration. In GN the problem is that less water gets filtered out, so it is retained. □ Protein — ✅ Yes — but only a moderate amount in GN (usually <3.5 g/day). Massive protein loss belongs to nephrotic syndrome. □ Red blood cells — ✅ Yes — this is the signature. RBCs and RBC casts in the urine turn it cola/tea colored. □ White blood cells — ✅ Yes, WBCs and casts appear because the glomerulus is inflamed.

STEP 1 Recent infection (group A beta-hemolytic strep — throat or skin — 1–3 weeks earlier) ➜ STEP 2 Immune response ➜ STEP 3 Antigen–antibody (immune) complexes form and deposit in the glomerular basement membrane, activating complement ➜ STEP 4 Inflammation of the glomerulus ➜ STEP 5 Filter becomes damaged ➜ STEP 6 RBCs and protein leak into the urine → hematuria and proteinuria ➜ STEP 7 GFR falls → sodium and water are retained → circulating volume expands ➜ STEP 8 Blood pressure increases

If the kidney filter is inflamed, would urine output increase or decrease? Decrease — oliguria. Explain WHY. Inflammation swells and narrows the glomerular capillary loops, so less plasma is filtered per minute (GFR drops). Less filtrate in = less urine out, and the salt and water that should have been excreted stay in the body → edema and hypertension.

entries.h: Recognizing the Patient — check all that support glomerulonephritis
entries.t: □ Periorbital edema — ✅ Classic — puffy face/eyes on waking, because retained fluid settles in loose tissue overnight □ Cola-colored urine — ✅ The hallmark — RBCs and RBC casts in the urine □ Hypertension — ✅ From sodium and water retention plus RAAS activation □ Proteinuria — ✅ Present, but mild-to-moderate (<3.5 g/day) □ Oliguria — ✅ GFR has fallen □ Weight gain — ✅ Fluid retention — daily weight is the most reliable measure of it Also expect: fatigue and malaise, headache, elevated BUN/creatinine, elevated ASO titer (evidence of recent strep), and low serum complement (C3).

Assessment finding Why does it happen? Edema The damaged glomerulus cannot excrete sodium and water, so volume expands and spills into the interstitium — worst where tissue is loose (around the eyes, in the morning) Hypertension Volume overload plus reduced renal perfusion, which activates RAAS → vasoconstriction and more sodium retention Cola-colored urine Red blood cells leak through the inflamed glomerular membrane; hemoglobin breaks down in acidic urine, turning it brown/tea/cola colored (rather than bright red) Oliguria Inflammation narrows the capillary loops → GFR drops →

entries.h: 🚨 Clinical Judgment — sudden dyspnea, crackles, SpO₂ 88%
entries.t: What complication is occurring? Acute pulmonary edema from fluid volume overload — the retained fluid has backed up into the lungs. (Circulatory overload can also push into heart failure.) What should the nurse do FIRST? Sit the patient upright in high Fowler's with the legs dependent and apply oxygen. That immediately reduces venous return and lets the diaphragm drop, so it improves oxygenation before any drug can. Then call the provider and anticipate IV furosemide, and keep the patient NPO/fluid-restricted.

Disease Acute glomerulonephritis ➜ Damaged structure The glomerulus — the filtering membrane itself ➜ Major symptoms Cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, hypertension, oliguria, weight gain, fatigue, mild proteinuria ➜ Priority care Blood pressure control, daily weights and strict I&O, sodium and fluid restriction, monitor respiratory status for overload, protein restriction if azotemic, antibiotics if strep is still present, rest 💬 Ask Claire: "Give me five patient scenarios with glomerulonephritis. Help me recognize the disease using only assessment findings. Make me explain WHY every symp

entries.h: Unit 10 · Nephrotic Syndrome — When the Filter Leaks Protein 🫧

entries.t: STEP 1 Damaged glomerulus ➜ STEP 2 Protein leaks into urine (>3.5 g/day — massive proteinuria, foamy urine) ➜ STEP 3 Blood loses albumin — and with it, plasma oncotic (pulling) pressure ➜ STEP 4 Fluid leaves the bloodstream ➜ STEP 5 Fluid enters tissues ➜ STEP 6 Massive generalized edema (anasarca) — and because the vascular space is now under-filled, RAAS turns on and retains even more salt and water Why is albumin important? Albumin is a sponge — it pulls water into the bloodstream. If albumin drops, the water leaves the vessels and moves into the interstitial tissue. That is why the swellin

entries.h: Assessment Detective — which patient has nephrotic syndrome?
entries.t: Patient A (cola-colored urine, hypertension, recent strep) — ❌ That is glomerulonephritis — blood is leaking, and there is a post-infectious trigger. Patient B (foamy urine, +4 pitting edema, albumin 2.1, proteinuria) — ✅ Nephrotic syndrome. Foam = protein in the urine; albumin 2.1 g/dL (normal 3.5–5.0) is the hypoalbuminemia; the +4 edema is the direct consequence of losing oncotic pressure.

Finding Why? Massive edema Low serum albumin → low plasma oncotic pressure → fluid shifts from vessels into tissue; RAAS activation then adds more sodium and water Foamy urine Protein in urine lowers its surface tension, so it froths in the toilet — the patient's own early warning sign Low albumin The damaged glomerular membrane lets albumin escape faster than the liver can replace it Hyperlipidemia The liver senses low oncotic pressure and ramps up production of all its proteins, including lipoproteins — and lipid clearance falls at the same time. Result: high cholesterol, high trig

Glomerulonephritis Nephrotic syndrome Blood in urine ✅ Yes — the defining feature. RBCs and RBC casts ❌ Usually minimal or absent Protein in urine Mild to moderate (<3.5 g/day) ✅ Massive (>3.5 g/day) — the defining feature Edema Present but usually mild–moderate; periorbital and facial, worse in the morning Severe and generalized — anasarca, ascites, +3/+4 pitting Hypertension ✅ Common and often severe — volume overload + RAAS Variable; may be normal or even low because the vascular space is under-filled Foamy urine ❌ Not typical ✅ Classic Cola urine ✅ Classic ❌ Not typical Serum albumin

entries.h: Priority Nursing Care — circle the priorities and say why
entries.t: Monitor blood pressure — ✅ Volume and RAAS shifts move the BP in both directions; ACE inhibitors/ARBs are used specifically to reduce proteinuria Daily weights — ✅ The single best measure of fluid status — 1 kg = 1 L. Same scale, same time, same clothing, after voiding Strict intake/output — ✅ Tells you whether the diuretic is working and whether output is keeping up with intake Assess edema — ✅ Grade and locate it; measure abdominal girth if ascites is present Monitor respiratory status — ✅ The one that outranks the rest — fluid moving into the lungs is the life-threatening turn Monitor album

Weight ↑5 kg · albumin 2.0 · BP 146/88 · lungs clear · +4 edema · urine 4+ protein Q1 — What assessment finding is expected? All of them, actually — the 4+ proteinuria with albumin 2.0 and +4 pitting edema is textbook nephrotic syndrome. The 5 kg gain equals about 5 L of retained fluid. Q2 — What complication is MOST likely if fluid keeps increasing? Pulmonary edema — the lungs are clear now , which is exactly why you keep listening. Pleural effusion, ascites, and worsening skin breakdown follow the same fluid. Q3 — Which intervention best evaluates treatment effectiveness? Daily weight,

entries.h: 🧠 Pattern Check — answer without looking back
entries.t: Cola-colored urine makes me think: Glomerulonephritis Foamy urine makes me think: Nephrotic syndrome (protein loss) Massive protein loss makes me think: Nephrotic syndrome — and hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, clotting risk Recent strep infection makes me think: Post-infectious acute glomerulonephritis (1–3 weeks later) Periorbital edema is commonly seen in: Both — but it is the classic morning finding of glomerulonephritis, and is part of the generalized edema of nephrotic syndrome The BEST way to monitor fluid status is: Daily weight on the same scale at the same time (1 kg = 1
Ask one question: what is leaking through the damaged glomerulus? Blood leaking → glomerulonephritis. Protein leaking → nephrotic syndrome.
Acute means it happened fast — hours to days. The good news: AKI is often reversible if the cause is found and treated early.

Before Blood flow → Prerenal — a perfusion problem; the kidney tissue is still healthy ➜ Inside Kidneys → Intrarenal — damage to the kidney tissue itself (tubules, glomeruli, interstitium) ➜ After Urine leaves kidneys → bladder → urethra → Postrenal — an obstruction anywhere downstream of the kidney

entries.h: AKI Detective — Scenario #1 (83 y/o, 4 days vomiting/diarrhea, BP 82/48, HR 122, dry skin, UOP 12 mL/hr)
entries.t: Are the kidneys damaged? YES / NO NO — not yet. The tissue is intact. Then WHY are they failing? They are not being perfused. GI losses dropped the circulating volume, the MAP fell below what the glomeruli need to filter, and filtration stopped. Fix the volume and the kidney works again — but if the hypoperfusion continues, prerenal AKI becomes acute tubular necrosis, and then it IS damage. 🩺 What do the kidneys need before they can filter? Blood flow. Without perfusion, even perfectly healthy kidneys cannot work.

entries.h: Scenario #2 — IV contrast; creatinine doubles overnight; urine output falls
entries.t: Before / Inside / After? Inside — intrarenal. Explain WHY. Contrast is a nephrotoxin: it constricts renal vessels and is directly toxic to tubular epithelium, producing acute tubular necrosis. The cells slough into the tubules and plug them. Other classic intrarenal causes: aminoglycosides, vancomycin, NSAIDs, rhabdomyolysis (myoglobin), transfusion reactions, glomerulonephritis, and prolonged prerenal ischemia.

entries.h: Scenario #3 — severe BPH, no urine for 18 hours, distended bladder, creatinine rising
entries.t: Before / Inside / After? After — postrenal. The prostate is blocking outflow, urine backs up, pressure rises to the kidney, and filtration stops. Healthy kidneys cannot make urine if urine cannot leave. Postrenal AKI is the most rapidly reversible type — if you catch it before the nephrons are destroyed.

Type What's wrong? Examples Prerenal (~60–70%) Not enough blood is reaching the kidney — a perfusion/volume problem. Tissue is intact. BUN:creatinine ratio >20:1; urine is concentrated with low sodium. Hemorrhage, vomiting/diarrhea, burns, dehydration, sepsis (vasodilation), heart failure and cardiogenic shock, anaphylaxis, renal artery stenosis, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors reducing glomerular pressure Intrarenal (~25–40%) The kidney tissue itself is damaged — most often acute tubular necrosis. Urine is dilute (SG near 1.010) with high urine sodium; muddy brown granular casts. IV con

entries.h: The Four Phases of AKI — follow the patient
entries.t: PHASE 1 Onset / Initiation — hours to 2 days from the insult until oliguria begins ➜ PHASE 2 Oliguric — 8–14 days; <400 mL/24 hr; the sickest phase ➜ PHASE 3 Diuretic — 1–3 weeks; 1–5+ L/day of dilute urine ➜ PHASE 4 Recovery — GFR climbs back; takes weeks to 12 months

entries.h: Phase 1 — Onset. Write three examples of something that damages the kidneys.
entries.t: 1. A hypotensive event — hemorrhage, sepsis, prolonged surgery, or severe dehydration 2. A nephrotoxin — IV contrast, gentamicin, vancomycin, NSAIDs, or chemotherapy 3. An obstruction — BPH with retention, bilateral stones, or a blocked catheter What assessment finding is MOST important during this phase? Urine output — hourly. A falling output (<0.5 mL/kg/hr or <30 mL/hr) is the earliest sign, and it appears before the creatinine moves. Catching it here is what makes AKI reversible.

entries.h: Phase 2 — Oliguric phase. Fill in the blanks.
entries.t: Urine output becomes low — oliguric, <400 mL/24 hr (or <0.5 mL/kg/hr); sometimes anuric <100 mL/24 hr Fluid begins to accumulate — weight gain, edema, JVD, hypertension Potassium becomes elevated — hyperkalemia, the killer of this phase Creatinine becomes elevated — and keeps climbing daily BUN becomes elevated — azotemia → nausea, confusion, itching The lungs may develop crackles → pulmonary edema The ECG may show tall peaked T waves, then a flattened P wave and widened QRS Bonus — acid–base: metabolic acidosis (retained H⁺, lost bicarbonate) → Kussmaul respirations, and

entries.h: Clinical Picture — weight gain, +3 edema, crackles, BP 186/98, UOP 180 mL today, K⁺ 6.5
entries.t: What is your FIRST concern? The potassium of 6.5 mEq/L. Put the patient on continuous cardiac monitoring, get a 12-lead, and notify the provider — anticipate IV calcium gluconate (cardiac membrane protection), then insulin + D50 and/or albuterol to shift K⁺ into cells, then sodium polystyrene sulfonate/patiromer or urgent dialysis to remove it. Crackles + 180 mL/day is the close second, and dialysis fixes both.

1 — Monitor ECG (with K⁺ 6.5 this is the assessment that detects lethal change in real time) 2 — Review potassium level (confirms and trends the threat, and guides treatment) 3 — Assess lung sounds (breathing — crackles mean overload has reached the alveoli) 4 — Assess for edema (part of the volume picture, but peripheral edema is not immediately dangerous) 5 — Strict intake and output (essential ongoing monitoring; results accumulate over hours) 6 — Obtain daily weight (the best fluid measure, but it is a once-a-day trend, not a rescue) Which intervention could save the patient's life TODAY?

entries.h: Unit 12 · The Diuretic Phase — The Fluid Management FLIP 🔄
entries.t: Students think: "The patient is peeing again, so they're better." Not so fast. 🩺 Think like the kidney — can they concentrate urine yet? YES / NO NO. The tubules recover their ability to filter before they recover their ability to concentrate . So the patient makes huge volumes of very dilute urine (specific gravity around 1.010) and dumps water and electrolytes they cannot afford to lose.

entries.h: ⭐ The flip — this is the highest-yield concept in AKI
entries.t: Oliguric phase Diuretic phase Urine output <400 mL/24 hr 1–5+ L/day of dilute urine Fluid problem Fluid volume OVERLOAD Fluid volume DEFICIT Potassium HIGH — hyperkalemia LOW — hypokalemia, plus hyponatremia Fluids RESTRICT — usually 24-hr output + ~500–600 mL insensible loss REPLACE — IV/oral fluid and electrolyte replacement Watch for Pulmonary edema, hypertension, lethal dysrhythmia from high K⁺ Hypotension, dehydration, hypovolemic shock, dysrhythmia from LOW K⁺, falls Diet Restrict potassium, sodium, phosphorus and protein Liberalize — potassium is now being replaced, not rest

entries.h: Why is this dangerous? — circle all that apply
entries.t: □ Dehydration — ✅ Losing liters of water a day with no ability to conserve it □ Hypotension — ✅ Falling intravascular volume → orthostasis, tachycardia, shock □ Hypokalemia — ✅ Potassium and sodium are dumped along with the water → flat T waves, U waves, weakness, dysrhythmias □ Fluid overload — ❌ That was the previous phase. Overload risk has flipped to deficit risk.

STEP 1 Kidneys begin recovering ➜ STEP 2 Large amounts of dilute urine ➜ STEP 3 Fluid leaves the body ➜ STEP 4 Blood pressure falls — with a compensatory tachycardia and orthostatic drops ➜ STEP 5 Electrolytes drop — hypokalemia and hyponatremia; replace and recheck

Daily weight — ✅ Now you are watching for weight LOSS that is too fast — more than ~0.5–1 kg/day means over-diuresis Blood pressure — ✅ Hypotension is the expected danger of this phase Potassium — ✅ It flipped — now the risk is hypokalemia; check for flat T waves, U waves, weak muscles, ileus Intake and output — ✅ Output can exceed intake by liters; replacement is calculated from these numbers Fall precautions — ✅ Weak, hypotensive, dizzy patient making frequent urgent trips to the bathroom — a fall waiting to happen Orthostatic blood pressure — ✅ The earliest objective sign of volume de

How long? Weeks to months — sometimes up to a year. GFR climbs back toward baseline, but some patients are left with a permanently reduced GFR and go on to develop CKD. Reflection — why is AKI potentially reversible while CKD is not? In AKI the nephrons are stunned or acutely injured, not gone — tubular cells can regenerate once the cause (low perfusion, toxin, obstruction) is removed. In CKD the nephrons are progressively destroyed and replaced by fibrous scar tissue, and nephrons do not regenerate . Treatment in CKD slows the loss; it does not restore it. Clinical Judgment Challenge — Four c

Students focus on the creatinine; experienced nurses focus on the patient. Is the patient making urine? Are they fluid overloaded? Can I hear crackles? Is the potassium dangerous? Is the heart at risk? The creatinine tells you how injured the kidney is — the assessment tells you how sick the patient is.

entries.h: Unit 13 · Chronic Kidney Disease — The Kidneys Are Tired 🏭
entries.t: 100 workers in a factory. One quits, the other 99 work harder. Then another. Then another. Eventually there aren't enough workers left to run the factory. That is CKD.

STEP 1 Healthy kidneys ➜ STEP 2 Some nephrons become damaged ➜ STEP 3 Remaining nephrons work harder — they hyperfiltrate to compensate, which is why labs stay normal for years… and that overwork eventually destroys them too ➜ STEP 4 More damage occurs ➜ STEP 5 GFR decreases — progressively and permanently ➜ STEP 6 Waste products accumulate — azotemia, then uremia when symptoms appear ➜ STEP 7 Kidneys can no longer maintain homeostasis ➜ STEP 8 End-Stage Kidney Disease Remember: CKD is progressive and irreversible — treatment slows progression, it does not cure. Definition: kidney damage or GF

entries.h: Why do people develop CKD? — which chronic diseases damage blood vessels?
entries.t: □ Diabetes — ✅ #1 cause. Chronic hyperglycemia thickens and scars the glomerular capillaries (diabetic nephropathy). Earliest sign: microalbuminuria. □ Hypertension — ✅ #2 cause. High pressure sclerose the small renal arterioles — and the damaged kidney then raises BP further, a vicious cycle. □ Lupus — ✅ Yes — lupus nephritis is immune-complex damage to the glomerulus □ Recurrent kidney infections — ✅ Yes — repeated pyelonephritis scars renal tissue permanently □ Polycystic kidney disease — ✅ Yes — the leading inherited cause; cysts replace functioning nephrons 🩺 Which two diseases cause MOST

entries.h: Stages of CKD — understand the trend
entries.t: Stage GFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) What is happening? Stage 1 >90 Kidney damage present (protein in the urine, or an abnormal scan) but normal GFR. Patient feels fine. Focus: treat the cause — glucose and BP control, stop nephrotoxins. Stage 2 60–89 (mild ↓) Mild loss with damage. Still usually asymptomatic. Estimate progression rate and keep protecting the kidney. Stage 3 (3a 45–59 / 3b 30–44) 30–59 (moderate ↓↓) The turning point — labs finally change. Creatinine and BUN rise; anemia, hyperphosphatemia and early bone disease begin. Start dietary restrictions, p

entries.h: Body System Challenge — CKD affects almost EVERY system. Why?
entries.t: System Finding → Why? 🧠 Brain Confusion. Uremic toxins cross into the CNS — uremic encephalopathy. Add anemia (less O₂ delivery) and electrolyte shifts. Progresses from foggy → lethargic → seizures. Peripheral neuropathy and restless legs come from the same toxins. ❤️ Heart Hypertension. Sodium and water retention expands volume, and the damaged kidney over-secretes renin → RAAS → vasoconstriction and aldosterone. The hypertension then damages the kidney further. Long term: LVH, heart failure, and — in late uremia — pericarditis with a friction rub. 🫁 Lungs Crackles. F

A Kidneys fail → potassium rises → heart becomes irritable → peaked T waves, dysrhythmias, arrest B Kidneys fail → fluid retained → lungs develop crackles and pulmonary edema; SpO₂ falls C Kidneys fail → erythropoietin decreases → bone marrow makes fewer red blood cells → patient becomes anemic — fatigued, pale, short of breath, tachycardic D Kidneys fail → vitamin D activation decreases → calcium falls (and phosphorus rises) → bones become weak, brittle and fracture easily — renal osteodystrophy NCLEX Pause — A client with Stage 5 CKD sud

entries.h: Unit 14 · Lab Detective — Can You Recognize CKD? 🧪
Patient A — Cr 0.9 · K⁺ 4.2 · Hgb 14 · GFR 98
entries.t: Healthy? YES / NO YES — every value is within normal limits: creatinine 0.6–1.2, potassium 3.5–5.0, hemoglobin 12–16 g/dL (women) / 14–18 (men), GFR >90.

entries.h: Patient B — Cr 4.9 · K⁺ 6.1 · Hgb 8.4 · phosphorus high · calcium low · GFR 11
entries.t: What disease? Stage 5 chronic kidney disease (end-stage renal disease). GFR 11 with that full constellation — azotemia, hyperkalemia, anemia, hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia together — is the fingerprint of CKD, not of a single acute event. Abnormal lab Explain it Creatinine 4.9 Muscle waste that only the kidney clears — a level this high means filtration has essentially stopped Potassium 6.1 The kidney normally excretes ~90% of daily potassium. It cannot, and the metabolic acidosis shifts even more K⁺ out of the cells. This is the one that can kill today. Hemoglobin 8.4 Loss of erythropoie

entries.h: Which Finding Worries You Most? — rank 1 (highest) to 5
entries.t: 1 — Potassium 6.4 (cardiac arrest risk in minutes — get an ECG) 2 — Calcium 7.8 (hypocalcemia → tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, prolonged QT — the second value with an acute neuromuscular/cardiac threat) 3 — Hemoglobin 8.5 (impairs oxygen delivery now; symptomatic, but treated over days–weeks with ESAs and iron) 4 — Creatinine 5.8 (tells you the severity of the disease; not directly dangerous) 5 — Phosphorus 6.2 (drives long-term bone disease and itching — a months-to-years problem; treat with binders taken WITH meals) Explain your ranking: Rank by how fast the value can kill. Elect

entries.h: The Nursing Process — what will you monitor every shift?
entries.t: ☐ Weight — ✅ Best single fluid indicator — same scale, same time, after voiding ☐ Lung sounds — ✅ Crackles are the earliest sign that overload reached the alveoli ☐ Intake/output — ✅ Guides the fluid restriction and shows whether they are still making urine ☐ Potassium — ✅ The lab with the shortest fuse ☐ Blood pressure — ✅ Both cause and consequence of kidney damage; control slows progression ☐ Mental status — ✅ New confusion = rising uremic toxins, or a dangerous electrolyte shift ☐ Skin — ✅ Itching, dryness, bruising and breakdown; edematous skin tears easily ☐ Edema — ✅ Grade and locate; c

1 CKD ➜ 2 Kidneys cannot… filter waste, excrete water and potassium, excrete acid, make erythropoietin, or activate vitamin D ➜ 3 Results in… azotemia/uremia, fluid overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia, hyperphosphatemia with hypocalcemia and bone disease, hypertension ➜ 4 Assessment findings… weight gain, edema, crackles, hypertension, peaked T waves, fatigue and pallor, itching, nausea, confusion, bone pain ➜ 5 Priority nursing care… monitor K⁺ and the ECG, daily weight and strict I&O, fluid and sodium/potassium/phosphorus restriction, protect the dialysis access, give binders

entries.h: Clinical Judgment Case — Mr. Lopez, dialysis tomorrow
entries.t: Weight ↑4 kg since last treatment · BP 192/102 · bibasilar crackles · +3 edema · K⁺ 6.3 · SpO₂ 90% Q1 — What concerns you MOST? Two findings are competing: the potassium of 6.3 and the SpO₂ of 90% with crackles. Assess the breathing first (ABCs — sit him up and give oxygen), but the potassium is the finding that will kill him fastest, so get the ECG and call immediately. Both point to the same answer: he needs dialysis today , not tomorrow. Q2 — What complication is developing? Fluid volume overload with pulmonary edema (4 kg = ~4 L retained), plus severe hyperkalemia — the classic missed

Crackles? → fluid overload. Anemia? → no erythropoietin. Weak bones? → no active vitamin D. Peaked T waves? → hyperkalemia. Confusion? → waste products building up. Itching? → uremic waste in the skin. Stop memorizing symptoms; connect each one back to a lost kidney function.

entries.h: Unit 15 · Dialysis — When the Kidneys Can't Do Their Job Anymore 🩸
entries.t: Dialysis does not fix the kidneys. It takes over some of their jobs — not all of them.

Kidney function Can dialysis do it? So what? Remove excess fluid ✅ YES — by ultrafiltration This is why weight drops during treatment; "dry weight" is the target Remove waste products ✅ YES — urea and creatinine diffuse across the membrane BUN and creatinine fall after each treatment Remove potassium ✅ YES Dialysis is the definitive treatment for hyperkalemia in ESRD Correct acid–base imbalance ✅ YES — bicarbonate in the dialysate buffers the acidosis pH and HCO₃⁻ improve after treatment Produce erythropoietin ❌ NO — that is a hormone the kidney makes , not a solute it removes Which is w

Hemodialysis Peritoneal dialysis Blood filtered by An artificial semipermeable membrane inside the dialyzer machine The client's own peritoneal membrane Frequency Usually 3 times/week, 3–5 hours per session Usually 4–5 exchanges/day (CAPD), or nightly on a cycler Requires Vascular access — AV fistula, AV graft, or central venous catheter A surgically placed peritoneal (Tenckhoff) catheter in the abdomen Speed of fluid removal Faster — large shifts in a few hours More gradual/gentle fluid removal — easier on the heart Main complications Hypotension, muscle cramps, disequilibrium syn

entries.h: Clinical Reasoning — who benefits from peritoneal dialysis?
entries.t: □ Lives several hours from a dialysis center — ✅ PD is done at home, so no thrice-weekly travel □ Wants more independence — ✅ Self-managed, flexible schedule, fewer dietary restrictions □ Has severe cardiovascular instability — ✅ The slow, continuous fluid removal avoids the abrupt volume shifts and hypotension that hemodialysis causes — much better tolerated by an unstable heart ⚠️ Who should NOT get PD? Patients with extensive abdominal adhesions or prior extensive abdominal surgery, active abdominal infection or peritonitis, hernias, severe obesity, or anyone who cannot maintain sterile tec

entries.h: Unit 15b · Peritoneal Dialysis — What Should Normal Look Like? 🚨
entries.t: STEP 1 — FILL Warmed dialysate infuses by gravity into the peritoneal cavity (~10 min) ➜ STEP 2 — DWELL Fluid sits; waste, K⁺ and water move across the peritoneum into the dialysate ➜ STEP 3 — DRAIN Bag lowered below the abdomen; effluent drains out by gravity ⚠️ Warm the dialysate with a dry heating pad or warmer — never in a microwave . Cold fluid causes pain and cramping; overheated fluid burns the peritoneum. Assessment Expected finding Drainage color Clear, pale yellow — like straw. (Slightly blood-tinged is acceptable only in the first few exchanges after catheter insertion.) Catheter si

entries.h: ⛔ STOP — the dialysate suddenly becomes cloudy
entries.t: First thought? PERITONITIS — cloudy effluent is the earliest and most reliable sign, and it usually appears before the fever. Why is this an emergency? The peritoneum is a huge, highly vascular surface with a catheter running straight into it from the outside. Infection there spreads to the bloodstream fast (sepsis), and repeated episodes scar the membrane so PD stops working permanently. Send effluent for cell count, Gram stain and culture, then give antibiotics — often added directly into the dialysate.

entries.h: Recognizing Peritonitis — circle every finding that concerns you
entries.t: □ Fever — ✅ Systemic infection □ Cloudy drainage — ✅ The hallmark and the earliest sign □ Clear yellow drainage — ❌ That is the normal, expected finding □ Abdominal pain — ✅ Diffuse pain with rebound tenderness — the peritoneum is inflamed □ Chills — ✅ Rigors point to bacteremia □ Redness around catheter — ✅ Exit-site infection — the usual doorway for peritonitis □ Bloody drainage — ✅ Concerning after the first few post-insertion exchanges — report it 🩺 Which finding should you report FIRST? The cloudy dialysate with abdominal pain — together they are diagnostic of peritonitis, and they show u

entries.h: Unit 15c · Hemodialysis & Vascular Access — Your Lifeline 🩸
entries.t: Without vascular access, there is no dialysis.

Access What it is Advantage Watch out AV fistula A surgeon connects the patient's own artery directly to a vein (usually radial artery to cephalic vein), and the vein enlarges and toughens Best long-term option — lowest infection and clotting rates, lasts the longest because it is all native tissue Needs 6 weeks to 4 months to mature before it can be used — so it must be placed well before dialysis is needed (stage 4) AV graft A synthetic tube is tunneled to join an artery and a vein when the patient's own vessels are too small or damaged Usable much sooner — about 2–4 weeks — and an opt

entries.h: Assessment Detective — your patient has an AV fistula
entries.t: I should FEEL a THRILL — a buzzing/purring vibration under your fingertips (palpate) I should HEAR a BRUIT — a swishing, whooshing sound with the bell of the stethoscope (auscultate) What if they're missing? The access is clotted or occluded. Also check for a cool, pale, numb or painful hand distal to the fistula — that is steal syndrome, where the fistula is diverting blood away from the hand. What does no thrill mean? Blood is not flowing through the fistula — it has thrombosed. Without it, the patient has no way to receive dialysis. What should the nurse do? Notify the provider/dialysis tea

entries.h: ❌ Protect the Access! — circle ALL actions that are NOT allowed
entries.t: Blood pressure on that arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — the cuff compresses the fistula and can clot it IV insertion in that arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — punctures introduce infection and damage the vessel Blood draws from that arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — same reason; use the other arm Palpate for thrill — ✅ Allowed — required, in fact, every shift Listen for bruit — ✅ Allowed — also required every shift Sleep on the access arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — hours of body weight on it can occlude it Carry heavy groceries with that arm — 🚫 NOT ALLOWED — heavy lifting and pressure compromise flow Wear tight clothing or jewelry on t

entries.h: Before Dialysis — check all that apply
entries.t: ☐ Weight — ✅ Pre-weight vs. dry weight determines how much fluid to pull off ☐ Blood pressure — ✅ Baseline for detecting the hypotension that fluid removal causes ☐ Potassium — ✅ Drives urgency and dialysate composition ☐ Medication list — ✅ Some drugs must be held; some must be redosed after ☐ Lung sounds — ✅ Baseline volume status ☐ Access site — ✅ Thrill, bruit, and signs of infection — no access, no treatment Which medications are commonly held before dialysis? Antihypertensives (and often other BP-lowering drugs), plus water-soluble medications that dialysis will simply remove — many anti

entries.h: During Dialysis — the blood pressure suddenly drops
entries.t: Why might this happen? Fluid is being removed from the vascular space faster than it can refill from the tissues → hypovolemia. Made worse by taking antihypertensives beforehand, eating during treatment (blood shunts to the gut), too aggressive an ultrafiltration goal, or an inaccurate dry weight. Also consider bleeding from the access and, rarely, a transfusion-type or air-embolism reaction. What assessment should you perform FIRST? Recheck the blood pressure and assess the patient's level of consciousness and symptoms (dizziness, nausea, cramping, pallor, diaphoresis). Then lower the he

entries.h: After Dialysis — what do you expect?
entries.t: Parameter Expected finding Weight ↓ DECREASED — typically 1–4 kg, matching the liters of fluid removed. This is the main measure of treatment effectiveness. Blood pressure ↓ DECREASED — watch for symptomatic hypotension and orthostasis Potassium ↓ DECREASED — back toward normal (sometimes low enough to matter, so recheck) BUN ↓ DECREASED Creatinine ↓ DECREASED — though not to normal; it rises again before the next treatment Hemoglobin Essentially unchanged or slightly lower — dialysis does not treat anemia and some blood is lost in the circuit Nursing priority —

entries.h: Complications — match the complication to its cause
entries.t: Complication Cause What you do Hypotension Rapid removal of fluid — the vascular space empties faster than it can refill Trendelenburg, slow/stop ultrafiltration, saline bolus per protocol, recheck BP Disequilibrium syndrome Rapid movement of water into brain cells — urea is cleared from the blood faster than from the CNS, so water follows the osmotic gradient into the brain → cerebral edema Slow or stop dialysis and notify the provider — prevented by short, slow initial treatments Access infection Redness, warmth, drainage — organisms entering at the needle/catheter site Culture, antibio

entries.h: ⛔ STOP & THINK — nausea → headache → confusion during dialysis
entries.t: What complication comes to mind? Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome. The classic progression is nausea → headache → restlessness → confusion → twitching → seizures. Most common during the first few treatments or when the BUN was very high. Why is this dangerous? It is cerebral edema. Urea leaves the blood quickly but lingers in brain tissue, so water is pulled into brain cells. Untreated it progresses to seizures, coma and death. Slow or stop the dialysis and notify the provider now.

entries.h: Clinical Judgment Case — Mr. Adams returns from dialysis
entries.t: BP 88/52 · HR 112 · dizzy · weight down 3 kg · AV fistula dressing dry Q1 — Why is his blood pressure low? Three liters of fluid were removed from his vascular space in a few hours (3 kg = 3 L). The intravascular volume dropped faster than fluid could shift back in from the tissues → hypovolemia, with the HR of 112 as the compensation. Q2 — What should the nurse do FIRST? Lie him flat and elevate his legs (or place in Trendelenburg) — it returns blood to the central circulation immediately and costs nothing. Then recheck BP and HR, keep him in bed, and notify the provider; anticipate a sm

entries.h: Compare These Patients — rank 1 (highest priority) to 4
entries.t: Patient D — K⁺ 6.8 with peaked T waves awaiting dialysis. #1 — lethal dysrhythmia possible within minutes; the ECG proves the heart is already affected. Patient A — Cloudy PD drainage, temp 101.9°F. #2 — peritonitis heading toward sepsis; needs cultures and antibiotics within the hour. Patient C — BP 86/48 after dialysis, dizzy when upright. #3 — a real perfusion problem and a fall risk, but it responds immediately to positioning and fluid. Patient B — No thrill over AV fistula. #4 — urgent (the access may be lost and dialysis delayed), but it is not killing anyone in the next ten minutes. Rea

Dialysis is not the answer to every problem. Sometimes the patient needs emergency treatment for hyperkalemia before dialysis, antibiotics for peritonitis, fluids after dialysis hypotension, or immediate evaluation of a nonfunctioning fistula. Assess the patient first, name the complication, then ask what could harm them fastest.
A transplant is life-changing — but it is not a cure. The body sees the new kidney as foreign and will try to attack it.

If your immune system attacks the new kidney, what is this called? Rejection. Hyperacute occurs within minutes to 48 hours (the organ must be removed); acute occurs within about the first week to 3 months and is often treatable; chronic occurs over months to years and gradually destroys the graft. How do we prevent it? Careful donor–recipient matching (ABO and HLA, plus a crossmatch) and lifelong immunosuppressant therapy — typically a calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine or tacrolimus) + an antiproliferative (mycophenolate) + a corticosteroid.

1 Healthy donor kidney ➜ 2 Surgery — the new kidney is placed in the iliac fossa (lower abdomen); the old kidneys usually stay in ➜ 3 Body recognizes new kidney as foreign ➜ 4 Immune system mounts an attack against the graft (rejection) ➜ 5 Patient must take immunosuppressants for life What if they stop taking them? The immune system reactivates and rejects the graft — the kidney fails and the patient goes back on dialysis, having burned a scarce organ. Nonadherence is one of the leading causes of late graft loss, so assess for cost barriers, side effects (hirsutism, gum overgrowth, tremor, we

entries.h: Nursing Priorities after Kidney Transplant — check them off
entries.t: ☐ Monitor urine output — ✅ The #1 indicator of graft function. Hourly at first; a sudden decrease is an early sign of rejection or of obstruction/thrombosis. ☐ Monitor for infection — ✅ Immunosuppression makes infection the leading cause of death after transplant — and the signs are blunted ☐ Encourage medication adherence — ✅ Lifelong, on schedule, never skipped — missed doses cost the kidney ☐ Teach low-sodium diet — ✅ Supports blood pressure control and protects the new kidney (steroids also cause sodium retention) ☐ Assess incision — ✅ Steroids and immunosuppressants delay healing and mask

entries.h: Why Are Transplant Patients So Vulnerable?
entries.t: Immunosuppressants decrease the body's ability to mount an immune response — to recognize and fight invading organisms and abnormal cells This places the patient at risk for infection (bacterial, viral — CMV, BK virus, herpes — and fungal), reactivation of latent infections such as TB, and long-term malignancy , especially skin cancer and lymphoma. Teach: avoid crowds and sick contacts, meticulous hand hygiene, no live vaccines, food safety, daily sunscreen, and report ANY fever right away.

Teach the client to avoid: ☐ Milk — ❌ Not a concern ☐ Grapefruit juice — ✅ AVOID. ☐ Bananas — ❌ Not related to cyclosporine (relevant to potassium counseling instead) ☐ Cranberry juice — ❌ Not a concern for this drug Why? Grapefruit inhibits the CYP3A4 enzyme that metabolizes cyclosporine, so drug levels climb into the toxic range → nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, tremor, hypertension and severe over-immunosuppression. The same warning applies to tacrolimus. Also teach: take at the same time every day, do not skip doses, expect gum overgrowth (see the dentist and brush meticulously) and h

entries.h: Unit 17 · Polycystic Kidney Disease — When Cysts Replace Healthy Kidneys 🧬
entries.t: Not an infection. Not a lifestyle disease. It is inherited — most commonly autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance.
1 Healthy nephrons ➜ 2 Fluid-filled cysts develop ➜ 3 Kidneys enlarge ➜ 4 Healthy tissue is replaced ➜ 5 Kidney function progressively declines → CKD → end-stage renal disease, usually by age 50–60

As cysts grow they squeeze the tiny vessels inside the kidney. What happens when blood flow decreases? The juxtaglomerular cells sense low renal perfusion — exactly as they would in hemorrhage — and switch on the RAAS. So the kidneys release: RENIN → angiotensin I → (ACE) angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor → aldosterone, which retains sodium and water; ADH is released too. What happens next? Blood pressure RISES — and the hypertension then damages the remaining nephrons, which further reduces perfusion, which releases more renin. A self-feeding loop. ⭐ Clinical Tip: the hy

Finding Why does it happen? Hypertension Cysts compress renal vessels → the kidney reads it as hypoperfusion → renin → RAAS → vasoconstriction + sodium/water retention. Present in most patients before the GFR even falls. Enlarged abdomen The kidneys can grow to many times normal size and become palpable bilaterally — abdominal fullness, early satiety, and a visibly protuberant abdomen Flank pain Stretching of the renal capsule by enlarging cysts, or pressure on surrounding structures — a dull, chronic ache Hematuria A cyst ruptures into the collecting system, or a stone pas

Dull, aching flank pain — Chronic pain from enlarging cysts stretching the renal capsule. Expected; managed with heat and non-nephrotoxic analgesia. Sharp, severe flank pain — Something acute: a ruptured cyst , a kidney stone , or an infected cyst. Look for new hematuria, fever, and hypotension — and report it.

entries.h: 🩺 Why is blood pressure the MOST important thing to monitor in PKD?
entries.t: Because controlling blood pressure is the one intervention that measurably slows the loss of kidney function. Uncontrolled hypertension accelerates nephron destruction, and PKD patients also carry a high rate of cerebral (berry) aneurysms — a hypertensive crisis can rupture one. So BP control protects both the kidneys and the brain. ACE inhibitors/ARBs are first line.

entries.h: Nursing Priorities — rank highest to lowest
entries.t: 1 — Monitor blood pressure (the intervention that changes the disease trajectory and prevents aneurysm rupture) 2 — Monitor renal labs (creatinine, BUN, GFR, K⁺ — detects decline and dangerous electrolytes) 3 — Assess pain (comfort, and a change in the pain pattern signals rupture, stone or infection) 4 — Monitor daily weights (fluid status as function declines) 5 — Encourage low-sodium diet (essential long-term teaching that supports BP control — but teaching ranks below monitoring an unstable parameter) Reasoning: Assessment and monitoring of the parameter that can cause acute harm come befo

entries.h: 🚨 Clinical Judgment — worsening headaches, blurred vision, BP 198/112
entries.t: What complication concerns you most? A hypertensive emergency — and specifically, in PKD, rupture of a cerebral (berry) aneurysm or hypertensive encephalopathy/stroke. Headache + visual changes + a diastolic over 110 is end-organ damage in progress. What should the nurse do FIRST? Notify the provider immediately and prepare for rapid, controlled BP reduction. Because this pressure is actively damaging the brain, eyes and kidneys right now. Meanwhile: keep the patient quiet with the head of bed elevated, do a neuro check, recheck the BP in both arms, and have seizure precautions and IV access r
Blowing up balloons inside a sponge. At first the sponge still works — but as more balloons grow, there isn't much sponge left.

1 Inherited genetic disorder ➜ 2 Fluid-filled cysts develop ➜ 3 Healthy nephrons become compressed and destroyed — replaced by cyst and scar tissue ➜ 4 Kidneys become enlarged — often massively, and palpable ➜ 5 Blood flow through the kidneys decreases ➜ 6 Blood pressure increases — via renin/RAAS ➜ 7 Kidney function gradually declines ➜ 8 Progressive kidney (renal) failure

entries.h: ⛔ Stop & Think — is PKD acute, chronic, congenital, or infectious?
entries.t: ☐ Acute — ❌ It develops over decades, not hours ☐ Chronic — ✅ Yes — slowly progressive and irreversible ☐ Congenital — ✅ Yes — the genetic defect is present from birth (inherited), even though symptoms usually appear in the 30s–40s ☐ Infectious — ❌ Not caused by an organism — though cysts can become infected as a complication 🩺 PKD develops over many years. Why don't patients get sick immediately? Because the kidney has enormous reserve. The undamaged nephrons hyperfiltrate and compensate, so labs and blood pressure stay normal until roughly half of function is gone. Symptoms typically s

entries.h: Why Is Blood Pressure So Important? — complete the pathway
entries.t: 1 Growing cysts ➜ 2 Compress renal blood vessels ➜ 3 Kidneys receive less blood flow / perfusion (oxygenated blood) ➜ 4 Kidneys think blood pressure is too LOW ➜ 5 RAAS is activated ➜ 6 Blood pressure increases — vasoconstriction plus sodium and water retention ➜ 7 Kidney damage accelerates — and the cycle repeats Clinical connection — why is BP control the top nursing priority? Because it is the only modifiable factor that slows the disease. Every year of uncontrolled hypertension destroys nephrons faster and moves the patient closer to dialysis, and it also raises the risk of rupturing a cer

entries.t: ☐ Flank pain — ✅ Dull and chronic from capsular stretch ☐ Enlarged abdomen — ✅ Bilaterally palpable, massively enlarged kidneys ☐ Hypertension — ✅ Usually the earliest sign of all ☐ Bloody urine — ✅ Gross or microscopic hematuria from cyst rupture ☐ Kidney stones — ✅ Common — urinary stasis and concentrated urine ☐ Constipation — ✅ Yes — the enlarged kidneys physically press on the bowel ☐ Progressive fatigue — ✅ From rising uremic toxins and anemia as function declines ☐ Frequent hypoglycemia — ❌ Not a feature of PKD. (Late kidney disease actually reduces insulin clearance, but hypoglycemia i

entries.h: Which Pain Is It? — part two
entries.t: "My side has been aching for weeks." — ☐ Enlarging cysts ☐ Ruptured cyst ✅ Enlarging cysts. Weeks of dull, gradual aching = slow capsular stretch. A rupture is sudden, not gradual. "It feels like someone stabbed me in my back." — ☐ Enlarging kidney ☐ Ruptured cyst ☐ Kidney stone ✅ Ruptured cyst or a kidney stone — both cause abrupt, severe pain. Sort them out with the pattern: a stone is colicky and radiates to the groin and the patient cannot sit still; a rupture is more constant flank pain with new gross hematuria. Either way, assess for bleeding, hypotension, fever and urine output, and not

Assessment finding Why does it happen? (say it in your own words) Hypertension Squeezed vessels → kidney thinks it is under-perfused → renin → RAAS → BP up Enlarged abdomen The kidneys themselves are the mass — cysts make them many times normal size Flank pain The renal capsule is being stretched from the inside Hematuria A cyst bleeds into the collecting system, or a stone scrapes the lining Kidney stones Stasis and distorted anatomy let minerals precipitate Progressive kidney failure Cysts physically replace working nephrons, and nephrons do not regenerate

entries.h: ⛔ STOP — your PKD patient's BP is 198/108. Just document it?
entries.t: YES / NO NO. Never document a pressure like this and walk away. Explain WHY. 198/108 is a hypertensive crisis in a patient who already has fragile renal vessels and an elevated risk of cerebral aneurysm. It is actively destroying nephrons and could cause a hemorrhagic stroke. Recheck manually, do a quick neuro and visual check, ask about headache/chest pain, look for missed antihypertensive doses, and notify the provider now.

entries.h: 💊 Medication Connection — the provider prescribes an NSAID for chronic flank pain
entries.t: Should the nurse question this order? YES / NO YES — question it. Why? NSAIDs are nephrotoxic . They block prostaglandins that keep the afferent arteriole dilated, so renal blood flow drops — exactly what a PKD kidney cannot afford — and they raise blood pressure and cause sodium retention. In a patient whose whole treatment plan is "protect perfusion and control BP," an NSAID works against both. Acetaminophen is the preferred analgesic in kidney disease.

BP 188/104 · dull bilateral flank pain · abdominal fullness · creatinine 2.8 mg/dL · bloody urine Q1 — Which finding concerns you MOST? The BP of 188/104. It is the only finding that can cause an acute catastrophe (stroke, aneurysm rupture) and it is the one accelerating everything else. The flank pain, fullness and hematuria are expected in PKD. Q2 — Greatest long-term risk? Progression to end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplant — typically by age 50–60, and sooner if the hypertension stays uncontrolled. His creatinine of 2.8 says he is already well into CKD. Q3 — What

entries.h: Unit 18 · Renal Calculi — When Urine Stops Flowing 🪨
entries.t: A pebble in a garden hose. Water may still flow at first — but as it moves it scrapes, pressure builds behind it, and the pain becomes intense. 💙 the tip: the pain is not the stone sitting in the kidney — it is the stone MOVING and blocking flow, making the ureter spasm.

Dilute urine keeps minerals in solution so they cannot crystallize, and the volume helps flush an existing stone downstream. entries.t: Stone location Pain pattern In the kidney Dull, deep, constant flank or CVA-area ache — often mild, and sometimes completely silent until the stone moves Moving through the ureter Severe, sharp, colicky flank pain in waves that radiates around the abdomen toward the groin — this is renal colic, the worst of it Near the bladder (UVJ) Radiates to the groin, testicles or labia and inner thigh, with urgency, frequency and dysuria — it feels like a UTI

Assessment finding Why does it happen? Hematuria The rough stone scrapes and tears the lining of the ureter as it travels Severe pain Ureteral spasm around the obstruction plus stretching of the renal capsule from back-pressure Nausea / vomiting The kidney and GI tract share autonomic innervation (celiac plexus), so intense renal pain triggers a vagal GI response — and may slow the bowel to a paralytic ileus Oliguria Obstruction is blocking urine flow. entries.h: ⛔ STOP — your patient suddenly stops producing urine
entries.t: What complication concerns you? Complete obstruction → hydronephrosis and postrenal AKI. In a patient with one functioning kidney, or with bilateral stones, anuria means total obstruction. Why is this an emergency? Urine backs up, the renal pelvis distends, and the pressure crushes the nephrons from the inside. Permanent damage begins within hours to a few days, and stagnant obstructed urine above an infection becomes urosepsis , which is rapidly fatal. Notify the provider immediately — the obstruction has to be relieved (stent or percutaneous nephrostomy), and no amount of pain medicatio

Test Why is it ordered? Urinalysis Detects hematuria (present in ~85–90%), crystals, and pH clues to stone type; WBCs and nitrites signal a concurrent infection — which changes everything about urgency CT scan (non-contrast helical) The gold standard — finds stones of nearly any composition, gives exact size and location, and shows hydronephrosis. No contrast is needed, which protects the kidney. Ultrasound No radiation and no contrast — preferred in pregnancy and for repeat monitoring. Shows hydronephrosis and stones in the kidney well; less reliable in the mid-ureter. KUB x-ray Cheap,

entries.t: 1 — Assess pain (assess before you intervene — and a sudden change in the pain tells you the stone moved or something ruptured) 2 — Administer prescribed analgesics (renal colic is one of the most severe pains in medicine; pain control is the priority intervention) 3 — Administer antiemetics (vomiting worsens dehydration and prevents oral fluids and meds) 4 — Strain all urine (every void, every time — a missed fragment means no stone analysis and no prevention plan) 5 — Encourage oral fluids (if appropriate) (possible once nausea is controlled; helps flush the stone) 6 — Encourage ambulation (
